# solana_program - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-program/

## Expand description

The base library for all Solana on-chain Rust programs.

All Solana Rust programs that run on-chain will link to this crate, which
acts as a standard library for Solana programs. Solana programs also link to
the [Rust standard library](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/), though it is [modified](https://solana.com/docs/programs/limitations#rust-libraries) for the
Solana runtime environment. While off-chain programs that interact with the
Solana network *can* link to this crate, they typically instead use the
[ solana-sdk](https://docs.rs/solana-sdk/latest/solana_sdk/) crate, which reexports all modules from

`solana-program`.This library defines

- macros for declaring the [program entrypoint](https://docs.rs#defining-a-solana-program),
- [core data types](https://docs.rs#core-data-types),
- [logging](https://docs.rs/log/index.html)macros,
- [serialization](https://docs.rs#serialization)methods,
- methods for [cross-program instruction execution](https://docs.rs#cross-program-instruction-execution),
- program IDs and instruction constructors for the system program and other
[native programs](https://docs.rs#native-programs),
- [sysvar](https://docs.rs/sysvar/index.html)accessors.

Idiomatic examples of `solana-program` usage can be found in
[the Solana Program Library](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana-program-library).

[§](https://docs.rs#defining-a-solana-program)Defining a solana program

Solana program crates have some unique properties compared to typical Rust programs:

- They are often compiled for both on-chain use and off-chain use. This is primarily because off-chain clients may need access to data types defined by the on-chain program.
- They do not define a `main`function, but instead define their entrypoint with the`entrypoint!`
- They are compiled as the [“cdylib”](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/linkage.html)crate type for dynamic loading by the Solana runtime.
- They run in a constrained VM environment, and while they do have access to
the [Rust standard library](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/), many features of the standard library, particularly related to OS services, will fail at runtime, will silently do nothing, or are not defined. See the[restrictions to the Rust standard library](https://solana.com/docs/programs/limitations#rust-libraries)in the Solana documentation for more.

Because multiple crates that are linked together cannot all define
program entrypoints (see the [ entrypoint!](https://docs.rs/macro.entrypoint.html) documentation) a common
convention is to use a

[Cargo feature](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/features.html)called

`no-entrypoint` to allow
the program entrypoint to be disabled.The skeleton of a Solana program typically looks like:

```
#[cfg(not(feature = "no-entrypoint"))]
pub mod entrypoint {
    use solana_program::{
        account_info::AccountInfo,
        entrypoint,
        entrypoint::ProgramResult,
        pubkey::Pubkey,
    };
    entrypoint!(process_instruction);
    pub fn process_instruction(
        program_id: &Pubkey,
        accounts: &[AccountInfo],
        instruction_data: &[u8],
    ) -> ProgramResult {
        // Decode and dispatch instructions here.
        todo!()
    }
}
// Additional code goes here.
```
With a `Cargo.toml` file that contains

```
[lib]
crate-type = ["cdylib"]
[features]
no-entrypoint = []
```
Note that a Solana program must specify its crate-type as “cdylib”, to
be discovered and built by the `cargo-build-sbf` command as a deployable program.
Solana programs also often have crate-type “rlib” so they can be linked to other Rust crates.
Avoid using “rlib” and “cdylib” crates together, since their combined usage precludes
compiler optimizations that may decrease program size and CU usage.

Prefer writing a separate package if it is supposed to be used as a library for other Solana programs (i.e. a “rlib” only crate). This would be normally the case for defining account types and helpers that are used by both clients and program. When creating a Rust project intended to be a program ready for deployment, use only the “cdylib” crate type.

[§](https://docs.rs#on-chain-vs-off-chain-compilation-targets)On-chain vs. off-chain compilation targets

Solana programs run on the [rbpf](https://github.com/solana-labs/rbpf) VM, which implements a variant of the
[eBPF](https://ebpf.io/) instruction set. Because this crate can be compiled for both on-chain
and off-chain execution, the environments of which are significantly
different, it extensively uses [conditional compilation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html) to tailor its
implementation to the environment. The `cfg` predicate used for identifying
compilation for on-chain programs is `target_os = "solana"`, as in this
example from the `solana-program` codebase that logs a message via a
syscall when run on-chain, and via a library call when offchain:

```
pub fn sol_log(message: &str) {
    #[cfg(target_os = "solana")]
    unsafe {
        sol_log_(message.as_ptr(), message.len() as u64);
    }
    #[cfg(not(target_os = "solana"))]
    program_stubs::sol_log(message);
}
```
This `cfg` pattern is suitable as well for user code that needs to work both
on-chain and off-chain.

`solana-program` and `solana-sdk` were previously a single crate. Because of
this history, and because of the dual-usage of `solana-program` for two
different environments, it contains some features that are not available to
on-chain programs at compile-time. It also contains some on-chain features
that will fail in off-chain scenarios at runtime. This distinction is not
well-reflected in the documentation.

For a more complete description of Solana’s implementation of eBPF and its
limitations, see the main Solana documentation for [on-chain programs](https://solana.com/docs/programs).

[§](https://docs.rs#core-data-types)Core data types

- `Pubkey`- [Solana account](https://solana.com/docs/core/accounts). Some account addresses are- [ed25519](https://ed25519.cr.yp.to/)public keys, with corresponding secret keys that are managed off-chain. Often, though, account addresses do not have corresponding secret keys — as with- *program derived addresses*- `Keypair`- `solana-program`but in- `solana-sdk`.
- `Hash`
- `AccountInfo`- `AccountInfo`.
- `Instruction`
- `ProgramError`- `ProgramResult`- `u64`.
- `Sol`- *lamports*- `native_token`

[§](https://docs.rs#serialization)Serialization

Within the Solana runtime, programs, and network, at least three different
serialization formats are used, and `solana-program` provides access to
those needed by programs.

In user-written Solana program code, serialization is primarily used for
accessing [ AccountInfo](https://docs.rs/sysvar/slot_history/struct.AccountInfo.html) data and

[data, both of which are program-specific binary data. Every program is free to decide their own serialization format, but data received from other sources —](https://docs.rs/instruction/struct.Instruction.html)

`Instruction`[sysvars](https://docs.rs/sysvar/index.html)for example — must be deserialized using the methods indicated by the documentation for that data or data type.

The three serialization formats in use in Solana are:

-
[Borsh](https://borsh.io/)[NEAR](https://near.org/)project, suitable for use in protocol definitions and for archival storage. It has a[Rust implementation](https://docs.rs/borsh)and a[JavaScript implementation](https://github.com/near/borsh-js)and is recommended for all purposes.Users need to import the `borsh``solana-program`, though this crate provides several useful utilities in its`borsh1`module`borsh`library.The `Instruction::new_with_borsh``Instruction`by serializing a value with borsh.
-
[Bincode](https://docs.rs/bincode)[Serde](https://serde.rs/)Rust APIs. As it does not have a specification nor a JavaScript implementation, and uses more CPU than borsh, it is not recommend for new code.Many system program and native program instructions are serialized with bincode, and it is used for other purposes in the runtime. In these cases Rust programmers are generally not directly exposed to the encoding format as it is hidden behind APIs. The `Instruction::new_with_bincode``Instruction`by serializing a value with bincode.
-
`Pack`[Solana Program Library](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana-program-library)to define their account format. It is difficult to implement and does not define a language-independent serialization format. It is not generally recommended for new code.

Developers should carefully consider the CPU cost of serialization, balanced against the need for correctness and ease of use: off-the-shelf serialization formats tend to be more expensive than carefully hand-written application-specific formats; but application-specific formats are more difficult to ensure the correctness of, and to provide multi-language implementations for. It is not uncommon for programs to pack and unpack their data with hand-written code.

[§](https://docs.rs#cross-program-instruction-execution)Cross-program instruction execution

Solana programs may call other programs, termed [ cross-program
invocation](https://docs.rs#cross-program-instruction-execution) (CPI), with the

[and](https://docs.rs/program/fn.invoke.html)

`invoke`[functions. When calling another program the caller must provide the](https://docs.rs/program/fn.invoke_signed.html)

`invoke_signed`[to be invoked, as well as the](https://docs.rs/instruction/struct.Instruction.html)

`Instruction`[for every account required by the instruction. Because the only way for a program to acquire](https://docs.rs/sysvar/slot_history/struct.AccountInfo.html)

`AccountInfo``AccountInfo` values is by receiving them from the runtime at the
[program entrypoint](https://docs.rs/macro.entrypoint.html), any account required by the callee program must transitively be required by the caller program, and provided by

*its*caller.

A simple example of transferring lamports via CPI:

```
use solana_account_info::{next_account_info, AccountInfo};
use solana_program_entrypoint::entrypoint;
use solana_program_error::ProgramResult;
use solana_cpi::invoke;
use solana_pubkey::Pubkey;
use solana_system_interface::instruction::transfer;
entrypoint!(process_instruction);
fn process_instruction(
    program_id: &Pubkey,
    accounts: &[AccountInfo],
    instruction_data: &[u8],
) -> ProgramResult {
    let account_info_iter = &mut accounts.iter();
    let payer = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    let recipient = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    assert!(payer.is_writable);
    assert!(payer.is_signer);
    assert!(recipient.is_writable);
    let lamports = 1000000;
    invoke(
        &transfer(payer.key, recipient.key, lamports),
        &[payer.clone(), recipient.clone()],
    )
}
```
Solana also includes a mechanism to let programs control and sign for
accounts without needing to protect a corresponding secret key, called
[ program derived addresses](https://solana.com/docs/core/cpi#program-derived-addresses). PDAs are derived with the

[function. With a PDA, a program can call](https://docs.rs/solana-address/1.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/solana_address/struct.Address.html#method.find_program_address)

`Pubkey::find_program_address``invoke_signed` to call another program while virtually “signing” for the
PDA.A simple example of creating an account for a PDA:

```
use solana_account_info::{next_account_info, AccountInfo};
use solana_program_entrypoint::entrypoint;
use solana_program_error::ProgramResult;
use solana_cpi::invoke_signed;
use solana_pubkey::Pubkey;
use solana_system_interface::instruction::create_account;
entrypoint!(process_instruction);
fn process_instruction(
    program_id: &Pubkey,
    accounts: &[AccountInfo],
    instruction_data: &[u8],
) -> ProgramResult {
    let account_info_iter = &mut accounts.iter();
    let payer = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    let vault_pda = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    let system_program = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    assert!(payer.is_writable);
    assert!(payer.is_signer);
    assert!(vault_pda.is_writable);
    assert_eq!(vault_pda.owner, &solana_system_interface::program::ID);
    assert!(solana_system_interface::program::check_id(system_program.key));
    let vault_bump_seed = instruction_data[0];
    let vault_seeds = &[b"vault", payer.key.as_ref(), &[vault_bump_seed]];
    let expected_vault_pda = Pubkey::create_program_address(vault_seeds, program_id)?;
    assert_eq!(vault_pda.key, &expected_vault_pda);
    let lamports = 10000000;
    let vault_size = 16;
    invoke_signed(
        &create_account(
            &payer.key,
            &vault_pda.key,
            lamports,
            vault_size,
            &program_id,
        ),
        &[
            payer.clone(),
            vault_pda.clone(),
        ],
        &[
            &[
                b"vault",
                payer.key.as_ref(),
                &[vault_bump_seed],
            ],
        ]
    )?;
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#native-programs)Native programs

Some solana programs are [ native programs](https://docs.solanalabs.com/runtime/programs), running native machine
code that is distributed with the runtime, with well-known program IDs.

Some native programs can be [invoked](https://docs.rs#cross-program-instruction-execution) by other programs, but some can
only be executed as “top-level” instructions included by off-chain clients
in a [ Transaction](https://docs.rs/solana-sdk/latest/solana_sdk/transaction/struct.Transaction.html).

This crate defines the program IDs for most native programs. Even though some native programs cannot be invoked by other programs, a Solana program may need access to their program IDs. For example, a program may need to verify that an ed25519 signature verification instruction was included in the same transaction as its own instruction. For many native programs, this crate also defines enums that represent the instructions they process, and constructors for building the instructions.

Locations of program IDs and instruction constructors are noted in the list below, as well as whether they are invokable by other programs.

While some native programs have been active since the genesis block, others
are activated dynamically after a specific [slot](https://solana.com/docs/terminology#slot), and some are not yet
active. This documentation does not distinguish which native programs are
active on any particular network. The `solana feature status` CLI command
can help in determining active features.

Native programs important to Solana program authors include:

-
**System Program**: Creates new accounts, allocates account data, assigns accounts to owning programs, transfers lamports from System Program owned accounts and pays transaction fees.- ID: `solana_system_interface::program::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_system_interface::instruction`
- Invokable by programs? yes

- ID:
-
**Compute Budget Program**: Requests additional CPU or memory resources for a transaction. This program does nothing when called from another program.- ID: `solana_compute_budget_interface::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_compute_budget_interface::ComputeBudgetInstruction`
- Invokable by programs? no

- ID:
-
**ed25519 Program**: Verifies an ed25519 signature.- ID: `solana_sdk_ids::ed25519_program::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_ed25519_program::new_ed25519_instruction_with_signature`
- Invokable by programs? no

- ID:
-
**secp256k1 Program**: Verifies secp256k1 public key recovery operations.- ID: `solana_sdk_ids::secp256k1_program::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_secp256k1_program::new_secp256k1_instruction_with_signature`
- Invokable by programs? no

- ID:
-
**BPF Loader**: Deploys, and executes immutable programs on the chain.- ID: `solana_sdk_ids::bpf_loader::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_loader_v2_interface::instruction`
- Invokable by programs? yes

- ID:
-
**Upgradable BPF Loader**: Deploys, upgrades, and executes upgradable programs on the chain.- ID: `solana_sdk_ids::bpf_loader_upgradeable::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_loader_v3_interface::instruction`
- Invokable by programs? yes

- ID:
-
**Deprecated BPF Loader**: Deploys, and executes immutable programs on the chain.- ID: `solana_sdk_ids::bpf_loader_deprecated::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_loader_v2_interface::instruction`
- Invokable by programs? yes

- ID:

- Same as `declare_sysvar_id`

- Convenience macro to declare a static address and functions to interact with it.
- [declare_](https://docs.rs/macro.declare_sysvar_id.html)- sysvar_ - id
- Declares an ID that implements `SysvarId`
- [entrypoint](https://docs.rs/macro.entrypoint.html)
- Declare the program entrypoint and set up global handlers.
- [entrypoint_](https://docs.rs/macro.entrypoint_deprecated.html)- deprecated
- Declare the program entrypoint.
- [entrypoint_](https://docs.rs/macro.entrypoint_no_alloc.html)- no_ - alloc
- Declare the program entrypoint and set up global handlers.
- [impl_](https://docs.rs/macro.impl_sysvar_get.html)- sysvar_ - get
- Implements the `Sysvar::get`
- [msg](https://docs.rs/macro.msg.html)
- Print a message to the log.
- [pubkey](https://docs.rs/macro.pubkey.html)
- Convenience macro to define a static `Address`value.
- [unchecked_](https://docs.rs/macro.unchecked_div_by_const.html)- div_ - by_ - const
- Convenience macro for doing integer division where the operation’s safety can be checked at compile-time.

# solana_program - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-program/4.0.0/solana_program/

## Expand description

The base library for all Solana on-chain Rust programs.

All Solana Rust programs that run on-chain will link to this crate, which
acts as a standard library for Solana programs. Solana programs also link to
the [Rust standard library](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/), though it is [modified](https://solana.com/docs/programs/limitations#rust-libraries) for the
Solana runtime environment. While off-chain programs that interact with the
Solana network *can* link to this crate, they typically instead use the
[ solana-sdk](https://docs.rs/solana-sdk/latest/solana_sdk/) crate, which reexports all modules from

`solana-program`.This library defines

- macros for declaring the [program entrypoint](https://docs.rs#defining-a-solana-program),
- [core data types](https://docs.rs#core-data-types),
- [logging](https://docs.rs/log/index.html)macros,
- [serialization](https://docs.rs#serialization)methods,
- methods for [cross-program instruction execution](https://docs.rs#cross-program-instruction-execution),
- program IDs and instruction constructors for the system program and other
[native programs](https://docs.rs#native-programs),
- [sysvar](https://docs.rs/sysvar/index.html)accessors.

Idiomatic examples of `solana-program` usage can be found in
[the Solana Program Library](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana-program-library).

[§](https://docs.rs#defining-a-solana-program)Defining a solana program

Solana program crates have some unique properties compared to typical Rust programs:

- They are often compiled for both on-chain use and off-chain use. This is primarily because off-chain clients may need access to data types defined by the on-chain program.
- They do not define a `main`function, but instead define their entrypoint with the`entrypoint!`
- They are compiled as the [“cdylib”](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/linkage.html)crate type for dynamic loading by the Solana runtime.
- They run in a constrained VM environment, and while they do have access to
the [Rust standard library](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/), many features of the standard library, particularly related to OS services, will fail at runtime, will silently do nothing, or are not defined. See the[restrictions to the Rust standard library](https://solana.com/docs/programs/limitations#rust-libraries)in the Solana documentation for more.

Because multiple crates that are linked together cannot all define
program entrypoints (see the [ entrypoint!](https://docs.rs/macro.entrypoint.html) documentation) a common
convention is to use a

[Cargo feature](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/features.html)called

`no-entrypoint` to allow
the program entrypoint to be disabled.The skeleton of a Solana program typically looks like:

```
#[cfg(not(feature = "no-entrypoint"))]
pub mod entrypoint {
    use solana_program::{
        account_info::AccountInfo,
        entrypoint,
        entrypoint::ProgramResult,
        pubkey::Pubkey,
    };
    entrypoint!(process_instruction);
    pub fn process_instruction(
        program_id: &Pubkey,
        accounts: &[AccountInfo],
        instruction_data: &[u8],
    ) -> ProgramResult {
        // Decode and dispatch instructions here.
        todo!()
    }
}
// Additional code goes here.
```
With a `Cargo.toml` file that contains

```
[lib]
crate-type = ["cdylib"]
[features]
no-entrypoint = []
```
Note that a Solana program must specify its crate-type as “cdylib”, to
be discovered and built by the `cargo-build-sbf` command as a deployable program.
Solana programs also often have crate-type “rlib” so they can be linked to other Rust crates.
Avoid using “rlib” and “cdylib” crates together, since their combined usage precludes
compiler optimizations that may decrease program size and CU usage.

Prefer writing a separate package if it is supposed to be used as a library for other Solana programs (i.e. a “rlib” only crate). This would be normally the case for defining account types and helpers that are used by both clients and program. When creating a Rust project intended to be a program ready for deployment, use only the “cdylib” crate type.

[§](https://docs.rs#on-chain-vs-off-chain-compilation-targets)On-chain vs. off-chain compilation targets

Solana programs run on the [rbpf](https://github.com/solana-labs/rbpf) VM, which implements a variant of the
[eBPF](https://ebpf.io/) instruction set. Because this crate can be compiled for both on-chain
and off-chain execution, the environments of which are significantly
different, it extensively uses [conditional compilation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html) to tailor its
implementation to the environment. The `cfg` predicate used for identifying
compilation for on-chain programs is `target_os = "solana"`, as in this
example from the `solana-program` codebase that logs a message via a
syscall when run on-chain, and via a library call when offchain:

```
pub fn sol_log(message: &str) {
    #[cfg(target_os = "solana")]
    unsafe {
        sol_log_(message.as_ptr(), message.len() as u64);
    }
    #[cfg(not(target_os = "solana"))]
    program_stubs::sol_log(message);
}
```
This `cfg` pattern is suitable as well for user code that needs to work both
on-chain and off-chain.

`solana-program` and `solana-sdk` were previously a single crate. Because of
this history, and because of the dual-usage of `solana-program` for two
different environments, it contains some features that are not available to
on-chain programs at compile-time. It also contains some on-chain features
that will fail in off-chain scenarios at runtime. This distinction is not
well-reflected in the documentation.

For a more complete description of Solana’s implementation of eBPF and its
limitations, see the main Solana documentation for [on-chain programs](https://solana.com/docs/programs).

[§](https://docs.rs#core-data-types)Core data types

- `Pubkey`- [Solana account](https://solana.com/docs/core/accounts). Some account addresses are- [ed25519](https://ed25519.cr.yp.to/)public keys, with corresponding secret keys that are managed off-chain. Often, though, account addresses do not have corresponding secret keys — as with- *program derived addresses*- `Keypair`- `solana-program`but in- `solana-sdk`.
- `Hash`
- `AccountInfo`- `AccountInfo`.
- `Instruction`
- `ProgramError`- `ProgramResult`- `u64`.
- `Sol`- *lamports*- `native_token`

[§](https://docs.rs#serialization)Serialization

Within the Solana runtime, programs, and network, at least three different
serialization formats are used, and `solana-program` provides access to
those needed by programs.

In user-written Solana program code, serialization is primarily used for
accessing [ AccountInfo](https://docs.rs/sysvar/slot_history/struct.AccountInfo.html) data and

[data, both of which are program-specific binary data. Every program is free to decide their own serialization format, but data received from other sources —](https://docs.rs/instruction/struct.Instruction.html)

`Instruction`[sysvars](https://docs.rs/sysvar/index.html)for example — must be deserialized using the methods indicated by the documentation for that data or data type.

The three serialization formats in use in Solana are:

-
[Borsh](https://borsh.io/)[NEAR](https://near.org/)project, suitable for use in protocol definitions and for archival storage. It has a[Rust implementation](https://docs.rs/borsh)and a[JavaScript implementation](https://github.com/near/borsh-js)and is recommended for all purposes.Users need to import the `borsh``solana-program`, though this crate provides several useful utilities in its`borsh1`module`borsh`library.The `Instruction::new_with_borsh``Instruction`by serializing a value with borsh.
-
[Bincode](https://docs.rs/bincode)[Serde](https://serde.rs/)Rust APIs. As it does not have a specification nor a JavaScript implementation, and uses more CPU than borsh, it is not recommend for new code.Many system program and native program instructions are serialized with bincode, and it is used for other purposes in the runtime. In these cases Rust programmers are generally not directly exposed to the encoding format as it is hidden behind APIs. The `Instruction::new_with_bincode``Instruction`by serializing a value with bincode.
-
`Pack`[Solana Program Library](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana-program-library)to define their account format. It is difficult to implement and does not define a language-independent serialization format. It is not generally recommended for new code.

Developers should carefully consider the CPU cost of serialization, balanced against the need for correctness and ease of use: off-the-shelf serialization formats tend to be more expensive than carefully hand-written application-specific formats; but application-specific formats are more difficult to ensure the correctness of, and to provide multi-language implementations for. It is not uncommon for programs to pack and unpack their data with hand-written code.

[§](https://docs.rs#cross-program-instruction-execution)Cross-program instruction execution

Solana programs may call other programs, termed [ cross-program
invocation](https://docs.rs#cross-program-instruction-execution) (CPI), with the

[and](https://docs.rs/program/fn.invoke.html)

`invoke`[functions. When calling another program the caller must provide the](https://docs.rs/program/fn.invoke_signed.html)

`invoke_signed`[to be invoked, as well as the](https://docs.rs/instruction/struct.Instruction.html)

`Instruction`[for every account required by the instruction. Because the only way for a program to acquire](https://docs.rs/sysvar/slot_history/struct.AccountInfo.html)

`AccountInfo``AccountInfo` values is by receiving them from the runtime at the
[program entrypoint](https://docs.rs/macro.entrypoint.html), any account required by the callee program must transitively be required by the caller program, and provided by

*its*caller.

A simple example of transferring lamports via CPI:

```
use solana_account_info::{next_account_info, AccountInfo};
use solana_program_entrypoint::entrypoint;
use solana_program_error::ProgramResult;
use solana_cpi::invoke;
use solana_pubkey::Pubkey;
use solana_system_interface::instruction::transfer;
entrypoint!(process_instruction);
fn process_instruction(
    program_id: &Pubkey,
    accounts: &[AccountInfo],
    instruction_data: &[u8],
) -> ProgramResult {
    let account_info_iter = &mut accounts.iter();
    let payer = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    let recipient = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    assert!(payer.is_writable);
    assert!(payer.is_signer);
    assert!(recipient.is_writable);
    let lamports = 1000000;
    invoke(
        &transfer(payer.key, recipient.key, lamports),
        &[payer.clone(), recipient.clone()],
    )
}
```
Solana also includes a mechanism to let programs control and sign for
accounts without needing to protect a corresponding secret key, called
[ program derived addresses](https://solana.com/docs/core/cpi#program-derived-addresses). PDAs are derived with the

[function. With a PDA, a program can call](https://docs.rs/solana-address/1.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/solana_address/struct.Address.html#method.find_program_address)

`Pubkey::find_program_address``invoke_signed` to call another program while virtually “signing” for the
PDA.A simple example of creating an account for a PDA:

```
use solana_account_info::{next_account_info, AccountInfo};
use solana_program_entrypoint::entrypoint;
use solana_program_error::ProgramResult;
use solana_cpi::invoke_signed;
use solana_pubkey::Pubkey;
use solana_system_interface::instruction::create_account;
entrypoint!(process_instruction);
fn process_instruction(
    program_id: &Pubkey,
    accounts: &[AccountInfo],
    instruction_data: &[u8],
) -> ProgramResult {
    let account_info_iter = &mut accounts.iter();
    let payer = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    let vault_pda = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    let system_program = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    assert!(payer.is_writable);
    assert!(payer.is_signer);
    assert!(vault_pda.is_writable);
    assert_eq!(vault_pda.owner, &solana_system_interface::program::ID);
    assert!(solana_system_interface::program::check_id(system_program.key));
    let vault_bump_seed = instruction_data[0];
    let vault_seeds = &[b"vault", payer.key.as_ref(), &[vault_bump_seed]];
    let expected_vault_pda = Pubkey::create_program_address(vault_seeds, program_id)?;
    assert_eq!(vault_pda.key, &expected_vault_pda);
    let lamports = 10000000;
    let vault_size = 16;
    invoke_signed(
        &create_account(
            &payer.key,
            &vault_pda.key,
            lamports,
            vault_size,
            &program_id,
        ),
        &[
            payer.clone(),
            vault_pda.clone(),
        ],
        &[
            &[
                b"vault",
                payer.key.as_ref(),
                &[vault_bump_seed],
            ],
        ]
    )?;
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#native-programs)Native programs

Some solana programs are [ native programs](https://docs.solanalabs.com/runtime/programs), running native machine
code that is distributed with the runtime, with well-known program IDs.

Some native programs can be [invoked](https://docs.rs#cross-program-instruction-execution) by other programs, but some can
only be executed as “top-level” instructions included by off-chain clients
in a [ Transaction](https://docs.rs/solana-sdk/latest/solana_sdk/transaction/struct.Transaction.html).

This crate defines the program IDs for most native programs. Even though some native programs cannot be invoked by other programs, a Solana program may need access to their program IDs. For example, a program may need to verify that an ed25519 signature verification instruction was included in the same transaction as its own instruction. For many native programs, this crate also defines enums that represent the instructions they process, and constructors for building the instructions.

Locations of program IDs and instruction constructors are noted in the list below, as well as whether they are invokable by other programs.

While some native programs have been active since the genesis block, others
are activated dynamically after a specific [slot](https://solana.com/docs/terminology#slot), and some are not yet
active. This documentation does not distinguish which native programs are
active on any particular network. The `solana feature status` CLI command
can help in determining active features.

Native programs important to Solana program authors include:

-
**System Program**: Creates new accounts, allocates account data, assigns accounts to owning programs, transfers lamports from System Program owned accounts and pays transaction fees.- ID: `solana_system_interface::program::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_system_interface::instruction`
- Invokable by programs? yes

- ID:
-
**Compute Budget Program**: Requests additional CPU or memory resources for a transaction. This program does nothing when called from another program.- ID: `solana_compute_budget_interface::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_compute_budget_interface::ComputeBudgetInstruction`
- Invokable by programs? no

- ID:
-
**ed25519 Program**: Verifies an ed25519 signature.- ID: `solana_sdk_ids::ed25519_program::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_ed25519_program::new_ed25519_instruction_with_signature`
- Invokable by programs? no

- ID:
-
**secp256k1 Program**: Verifies secp256k1 public key recovery operations.- ID: `solana_sdk_ids::secp256k1_program::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_secp256k1_program::new_secp256k1_instruction_with_signature`
- Invokable by programs? no

- ID:
-
**BPF Loader**: Deploys, and executes immutable programs on the chain.- ID: `solana_sdk_ids::bpf_loader::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_loader_v2_interface::instruction`
- Invokable by programs? yes

- ID:
-
**Upgradable BPF Loader**: Deploys, upgrades, and executes upgradable programs on the chain.- ID: `solana_sdk_ids::bpf_loader_upgradeable::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_loader_v3_interface::instruction`
- Invokable by programs? yes

- ID:
-
**Deprecated BPF Loader**: Deploys, and executes immutable programs on the chain.- ID: `solana_sdk_ids::bpf_loader_deprecated::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_loader_v2_interface::instruction`
- Invokable by programs? yes

- ID:

- [ed25519_](https://docs.rs/ed25519_program/index.html)- program

- [entrypoint_](https://docs.rs/entrypoint_deprecated/index.html)- deprecated
- The Rust-based BPF program entrypoint supported by the original BPF loader.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_heap_default.html)- heap_ - default
- Define the default global allocator.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_panic_default.html)- panic_ - default
- Define the default global panic handler.
- [declare_](https://docs.rs/macro.declare_deprecated_id.html)- deprecated_ - id
- Same as `declare_id`
- [declare_](https://docs.rs/macro.declare_deprecated_sysvar_id.html)- deprecated_ - sysvar_ - id
- Same as `declare_sysvar_id`
- [declare_](https://docs.rs/macro.declare_id.html)- id
- Convenience macro to declare a static address and functions to interact with it.
- [declare_](https://docs.rs/macro.declare_sysvar_id.html)- sysvar_ - id
- Declares an ID that implements `SysvarId`
- [entrypoint](https://docs.rs/macro.entrypoint.html)
- Declare the program entrypoint and set up global handlers.
- [entrypoint_](https://docs.rs/macro.entrypoint_deprecated.html)- deprecated
- Declare the program entrypoint.
- [entrypoint_](https://docs.rs/macro.entrypoint_no_alloc.html)- no_ - alloc
- Declare the program entrypoint and set up global handlers.
- [impl_](https://docs.rs/macro.impl_sysvar_get.html)- sysvar_ - get
- Implements the `Sysvar::get`
- [msg](https://docs.rs/macro.msg.html)
- Print a message to the log.
- [pubkey](https://docs.rs/macro.pubkey.html)
- Convenience macro to define a static `Address`value.
- [unchecked_](https://docs.rs/macro.unchecked_div_by_const.html)- div_ - by_ - const
- Convenience macro for doing integer division where the operation’s safety can be checked at compile-time.

# solana-program 4.0.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/solana-program/latest

# Solana Program

Use the Solana Program Crate to write on-chain programs in Rust.  If writing client-side applications, use the [Solana SDK Crate](https://crates.io/crates/solana-sdk) instead.

More information about Solana is available in the [Solana documentation](https://solana.com/docs).

[Solana Program Library](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana-program-library) provides examples of how to use this crate.

Still have questions?  Ask us on [Stack Exchange](https://sola.na/sse)

# memoffset - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/memoffset/^0.9/

## Expand description

A crate used for calculating offsets of struct members and their spans.

This functionality currently can not be used in compile time code such as `const` or `const fn` definitions.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use memoffset::{offset_of, span_of};
#[repr(C, packed)]
struct HelpMeIAmTrappedInAStructFactory {
    help_me_before_they_: [u8; 15],
    a: u32
}
assert_eq!(offset_of!(HelpMeIAmTrappedInAStructFactory, a), 15);
assert_eq!(span_of!(HelpMeIAmTrappedInAStructFactory, a), 15..19);
assert_eq!(span_of!(HelpMeIAmTrappedInAStructFactory, help_me_before_they_ .. a), 0..15);
```
This functionality can be useful, for example, for checksum calculations:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[repr(C, packed)]
struct Message {
    header: MessageHeader,
    fragment_index: u32,
    fragment_count: u32,
    payload: [u8; 1024],
    checksum: u16
}
let checksum_range = &raw[span_of!(Message, header..checksum)];
let checksum = crc16(checksum_range);
```
## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [offset_](https://docs.rs/macro.offset_of.html)- of
- Calculates the offset of the specified field from the start of the named struct.
- [offset_](https://docs.rs/macro.offset_of_tuple.html)- of_ - tuple
- Calculates the offset of the specified field from the start of the tuple.
- [offset_](https://docs.rs/macro.offset_of_union.html)- of_ - union
- Calculates the offset of the specified union member from the start of the union.
- [raw_](https://docs.rs/macro.raw_field.html)- field
- Computes a const raw pointer to the given field of the given base pointer to the given parent type.
- [raw_](https://docs.rs/macro.raw_field_tuple.html)- field_ - tuple
- Computes a const raw pointer to the given field of the given base pointer to the given parent tuple type.
- [raw_](https://docs.rs/macro.raw_field_union.html)- field_ - union
- Computes a const raw pointer to the given field of the given base pointer to the given parent tuple type.
- [span_of](https://docs.rs/macro.span_of.html)
- Produces a range instance representing the sub-slice containing the specified member.

# solana_cpi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-cpi/^3.0.0/

## Expand description

Cross-program invocation.

Solana programs may call other programs, termed [ cross-program
invocations](https://solana.com/docs/core/cpi) (CPI), with the

[and](https://docs.rs/fn.invoke.html)

`invoke`[functions.](https://docs.rs/fn.invoke_signed.html)

`invoke_signed`This crate does not support overwriting syscall stubs for offchain code.
If you want to overwrite syscall stubs, use the wrapper functions in
[ solana_program::program](https://docs.rs/solana-program/latest/solana_program/program/).

- [invoke](https://docs.rs/fn.invoke.html)
- Invoke a cross-program instruction.
- [invoke_](https://docs.rs/fn.invoke_signed.html)- signed
- Invoke a cross-program instruction with program signatures.
- [invoke_](https://docs.rs/fn.invoke_signed_unchecked.html)- signed_ - unchecked

- [invoke_](https://docs.rs/fn.invoke_unchecked.html)- unchecked
- Invoke a cross-program instruction but don’t enforce Rust’s aliasing rules.
- [set_](https://docs.rs/fn.set_return_data.html)- return_ - data
- Set the running program’s return data.

# solana_epoch_schedule - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-epoch-schedule/^3.0.0/

## Expand description

Configuration for epochs and slots.

Epochs mark a period of time composed of *slots*, for which a particular
[leader schedule](https://docs.solanalabs.com/consensus/leader-rotation#leader-schedule-rotation) is in effect. The epoch schedule determines the length
of epochs, and the timing of the next leader-schedule selection.

The epoch schedule does not change during the life of a blockchain,
though the length of an epoch does — during the initial launch of
the chain there is a “warmup” period, where epochs are short, with subsequent
epochs increasing in slots until they last for [ DEFAULT_SLOTS_PER_EPOCH](https://docs.rs/solana-clock/latest/solana_clock/constant.DEFAULT_SLOTS_PER_EPOCH.html).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_LEADER_SCHEDULE_SLOT_OFFSET.html)- LEADER_ - SCHEDULE_ - SLOT_ - OFFSET
- The default number of slots before an epoch starts to calculate the leader schedule.
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_LEADER_SCHEDULE_EPOCH_OFFSET.html)- LEADER_ - SCHEDULE_ - EPOCH_ - OFFSET
- The maximum number of slots before an epoch starts to calculate the leader schedule.
- [MINIMUM_](https://docs.rs/constant.MINIMUM_SLOTS_PER_EPOCH.html)- SLOTS_ - PER_ - EPOCH
- The minimum number of slots per epoch during the warmup period.
- [SIZE](https://docs.rs/constant.SIZE.html)
- Serialized size of the `EpochSchedule`sysvar account.

# solana_instruction - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-instruction/^3.0.0/

## Expand description

Types for directing the execution of Solana programs.

Every invocation of a Solana program executes a single instruction, as
defined by the [ Instruction](https://docs.rs/struct.Instruction.html) type. An instruction is primarily a vector of
bytes, the contents of which are program-specific, and not interpreted by
the Solana runtime. This allows flexibility in how programs behave, how they
are controlled by client software, and what data encodings they use.

Besides the instruction data, every account a program may read or write
while executing a given instruction is also included in `Instruction`, as
[ AccountMeta](https://docs.rs/account_meta/struct.AccountMeta.html) values. The runtime uses this information to efficiently
schedule execution of transactions.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use account_meta::`- [AccountMeta](https://docs.rs/account_meta/struct.AccountMeta.html);
- `pub use`- [solana_instruction_error](https://docs.rs/solana-instruction-error/2.2.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/solana_instruction_error/index.html)as error;

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [account_](https://docs.rs/account_meta/index.html)- meta
- [syscalls](https://docs.rs/syscalls/index.html)- `syscalls`or- `target_os=solana`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Borrowed](https://docs.rs/struct.BorrowedAccountMeta.html)- Account - Meta
- Borrowed version of `AccountMeta`.
- [Borrowed](https://docs.rs/struct.BorrowedInstruction.html)- Instruction
- Borrowed version of `Instruction`.
- [Instruction](https://docs.rs/struct.Instruction.html)
- A directive for a single invocation of a Solana program.
- [Processed](https://docs.rs/struct.ProcessedSiblingInstruction.html)- Sibling - Instruction
- Use to query and convey information about the sibling instruction components
when calling the `sol_get_processed_sibling_instruction`syscall.

---

# solana_instructions_sysvar - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-instructions-sysvar/^3.0.0/

## Expand description

The serialized instructions of the current transaction.

The *instructions sysvar* provides access to the serialized instruction data
for the currently-running transaction. This allows for [instruction
introspection](https://docs.solanalabs.com/implemented-proposals/instruction_introspection), which is required for correctly interoperating with
native programs like the [secp256k1](https://docs.rs/solana-secp256k1-program/latest/solana_secp256k1_program/) and [ed25519](https://docs.rs/solana-ed25519-program/latest/solana_ed25519_program/) programs.

Unlike other sysvars, the data in the instructions sysvar is not accessed
through a type that implements the [ Sysvar](https://docs.rs/solana-sysvar/latest/solana_sysvar/trait.Sysvar.html) trait. Instead, the
instruction sysvar is accessed through several free functions within this
module.

See also the Solana [documentation on the instructions sysvar](https://docs.solanalabs.com/runtime/sysvars#instructions).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

For a complete example of how the instructions sysvar is used see the
documentation for [ secp256k1_instruction](https://docs.rs/solana-sdk/latest/solana_sdk/secp256k1_instruction/index.html) in the

`solana-sdk` crate.## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Instructions](https://docs.rs/struct.Instructions.html)
- Instructions sysvar, dummy type.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [ID](https://docs.rs/constant.ID.html)
- The const program ID.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_id.html)- id
- Returns `true`if given address is the ID.
- [construct_](https://docs.rs/fn.construct_instructions_data.html)- instructions_ - data - Non- - `target_os=solana`
- Construct the account data for the instructions sysvar.
- [deserialize_](https://docs.rs/fn.deserialize_instruction.html)- instruction
- [get_](https://docs.rs/fn.get_instruction_relative.html)- instruction_ - relative
- Returns the `Instruction`relative to the current`Instruction`in the currently executing`Transaction`.
- [id](https://docs.rs/fn.id.html)
- Returns the ID.
- [load_](https://docs.rs/fn.load_current_index_checked.html)- current_ - index_ - checked
- Load the current `Instruction`’s index in the currently executing`Transaction`.
- [load_](https://docs.rs/fn.load_instruction_at.html)- instruction_ - at
- Load an `Instruction`in the currently executing`Transaction`at the specified index.
- [load_](https://docs.rs/fn.load_instruction_at_checked.html)- instruction_ - at_ - checked
- Load an `Instruction`in the currently executing`Transaction`at the specified index.
- [serialize_](https://docs.rs/fn.serialize_instructions.html)- instructions
- [store_](https://docs.rs/fn.store_current_index_checked.html)- current_ - index_ - checked
- Store the current `Instruction`’s index in the instructions sysvar data.

# solana_program_pack - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-program-pack/^3.0.0/

## Expand description

The [ Pack](https://docs.rs/trait.Pack.html) serialization trait
This is a specific serialization API that is used by many older programs in
the

[Solana Program Library](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana-program-library)to manage account state. It is not generally recommended for new code since it does not define a language-independent serialization format.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [IsInitialized](https://docs.rs/trait.IsInitialized.html)
- Check if a program account state is initialized
- [Pack](https://docs.rs/trait.Pack.html)
- Safely and efficiently (de)serialize account state
- [Sealed](https://docs.rs/trait.Sealed.html)
- Implementors must have a known size

# solana_secp256k1_recover - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-secp256k1-recover/^3.0.0/

## Expand description

Public key recovery from [secp256k1](https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Secp256k1) ECDSA signatures.

*This module provides low-level cryptographic building blocks that must be
used carefully to ensure proper security. Read this documentation and
accompanying links thoroughly.*

The [ secp256k1_recover](https://docs.rs/fn.secp256k1_recover.html) syscall allows a secp256k1 public key that has
previously signed a message to be recovered from the combination of the
message, the signature, and a recovery ID. The recovery ID is generated
during signing.

Use cases for `secp256k1_recover` include:

- Implementing the Ethereum `ecrecover`
- Performing secp256k1 public key recovery generally.
- Verifying a single secp256k1 signature.

While `secp256k1_recover` can be used to verify secp256k1 signatures, Solana
also provides the [secp256k1 program](https://docs.rs/solana-program/latest/solana_program/secp256k1_program/), which is more flexible, has lower CPU
cost, and can validate many signatures at once.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [secp256k1_](https://docs.rs/fn.secp256k1_recover.html)- recover
- Recover the public key from a [secp256k1](https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Secp256k1)ECDSA signature and cryptographically-hashed message.

- Same as u16, but serialized with 1 to 3 bytes. If the value is above 0x7f, the top bit is set and the remaining value is stored in the next bytes. Each byte follows the same pattern until the 3rd byte. The 3rd byte may only have the 2 least-significant bits set, otherwise the encoded value will overflow the u16.

# solana_sysvar - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-sysvar/^4.0.0/

## Expand description

Access to special accounts with dynamically-updated data.

Sysvars are special accounts that contain dynamically-updated data about the
network cluster, the blockchain history, and the executing transaction. Each
sysvar is defined in its own submodule within this module. The [ clock](https://docs.rs/clock/index.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/epoch_schedule/index.html)

`epoch_schedule`[sysvars are most useful to on-chain programs.](https://docs.rs/rent/index.html)

`rent`Simple sysvars implement the [ Sysvar::get](https://docs.rs/trait.Sysvar.html#method.get) method, which loads a sysvar
directly from the runtime, as in this example that logs the

`clock` sysvar:```
use solana_account_info::AccountInfo;
use solana_msg::msg;
use solana_sysvar::Sysvar;
use solana_program_error::ProgramResult;
use solana_pubkey::Pubkey;
fn process_instruction(
    program_id: &Pubkey,
    accounts: &[AccountInfo],
    instruction_data: &[u8],
) -> ProgramResult {
    let clock = solana_clock::Clock::get()?;
    msg!("clock: {:#?}", clock);
    Ok(())
}
```
Since Solana sysvars are accounts, if the `AccountInfo` is provided to the
program, then the program can deserialize the sysvar with
[ SysvarSerialize::from_account_info](https://docs.rs/trait.SysvarSerialize.html#method.from_account_info) to access its data, as in this example that
again logs the

[sysvar.](https://docs.rs/clock/index.html)

`clock````
use solana_account_info::{AccountInfo, next_account_info};
use solana_msg::msg;
use solana_sysvar::{Sysvar, SysvarSerialize};
use solana_program_error::ProgramResult;
use solana_pubkey::Pubkey;
fn process_instruction(
    program_id: &Pubkey,
    accounts: &[AccountInfo],
    instruction_data: &[u8],
) -> ProgramResult {
    let account_info_iter = &mut accounts.iter();
    let clock_account = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    let clock = solana_clock::Clock::from_account_info(&clock_account)?;
    msg!("clock: {:#?}", clock);
    Ok(())
}
```
When possible, programs should prefer to call `Sysvar::get` instead of
deserializing with `Sysvar::from_account_info`, as the latter imposes extra
overhead of deserialization while also requiring the sysvar account address
be passed to the program, wasting the limited space available to
transactions. Deserializing sysvars that can instead be retrieved with
`Sysvar::get` should be only be considered for compatibility with older
programs that pass around sysvar accounts.

Some sysvars are too large to deserialize within a program, and
`Sysvar::from_account_info` returns an error, or the serialization attempt
will exhaust the program’s compute budget. Some sysvars do not implement
`Sysvar::get` and return an error. Some sysvars have custom deserializers
that do not implement the `Sysvar` trait. These cases are documented in the
modules for individual sysvars.

All sysvar accounts are owned by the account identified by [ sysvar::ID](https://docs.rs/solana-sdk-ids/latest/solana_sdk_ids/sysvar/constant.ID.html).

For more details see the Solana [documentation on sysvars](https://docs.solanalabs.com/runtime/sysvars).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

# solana_example_mocks - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-example-mocks/^4.0.0/

## Expand description

Mock types for use in examples.

These represent APIs from crates that themselves depend on this crate, and which are useful for illustrating the examples for APIs in this crate.

Directly depending on these crates though would cause problematic circular dependencies, so instead they are mocked out here in a way that allows examples to appear to use crates that this crate must not depend on.

Each mod here has the name of a crate, so that examples can be structured to appear to import from that crate.

# solana_program - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/solana-program/latest/target-redirect/solana_program/

## Expand description

The base library for all Solana on-chain Rust programs.

All Solana Rust programs that run on-chain will link to this crate, which
acts as a standard library for Solana programs. Solana programs also link to
the [Rust standard library](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/), though it is [modified](https://solana.com/docs/programs/limitations#rust-libraries) for the
Solana runtime environment. While off-chain programs that interact with the
Solana network *can* link to this crate, they typically instead use the
[ solana-sdk](https://docs.rs/solana-sdk/latest/solana_sdk/) crate, which reexports all modules from

`solana-program`.This library defines

- macros for declaring the [program entrypoint](https://docs.rs#defining-a-solana-program),
- [core data types](https://docs.rs#core-data-types),
- [logging](https://docs.rs/log/index.html)macros,
- [serialization](https://docs.rs#serialization)methods,
- methods for [cross-program instruction execution](https://docs.rs#cross-program-instruction-execution),
- program IDs and instruction constructors for the system program and other
[native programs](https://docs.rs#native-programs),
- [sysvar](https://docs.rs/sysvar/index.html)accessors.

Idiomatic examples of `solana-program` usage can be found in
[the Solana Program Library](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana-program-library).

[§](https://docs.rs#defining-a-solana-program)Defining a solana program

Solana program crates have some unique properties compared to typical Rust programs:

- They are often compiled for both on-chain use and off-chain use. This is primarily because off-chain clients may need access to data types defined by the on-chain program.
- They do not define a `main`function, but instead define their entrypoint with the`entrypoint!`
- They are compiled as the [“cdylib”](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/linkage.html)crate type for dynamic loading by the Solana runtime.
- They run in a constrained VM environment, and while they do have access to
the [Rust standard library](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/), many features of the standard library, particularly related to OS services, will fail at runtime, will silently do nothing, or are not defined. See the[restrictions to the Rust standard library](https://solana.com/docs/programs/limitations#rust-libraries)in the Solana documentation for more.

Because multiple crates that are linked together cannot all define
program entrypoints (see the [ entrypoint!](https://docs.rs/macro.entrypoint.html) documentation) a common
convention is to use a

[Cargo feature](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/features.html)called

`no-entrypoint` to allow
the program entrypoint to be disabled.The skeleton of a Solana program typically looks like:

```
#[cfg(not(feature = "no-entrypoint"))]
pub mod entrypoint {
    use solana_program::{
        account_info::AccountInfo,
        entrypoint,
        entrypoint::ProgramResult,
        pubkey::Pubkey,
    };
    entrypoint!(process_instruction);
    pub fn process_instruction(
        program_id: &Pubkey,
        accounts: &[AccountInfo],
        instruction_data: &[u8],
    ) -> ProgramResult {
        // Decode and dispatch instructions here.
        todo!()
    }
}
// Additional code goes here.
```
With a `Cargo.toml` file that contains

```
[lib]
crate-type = ["cdylib"]
[features]
no-entrypoint = []
```
Note that a Solana program must specify its crate-type as “cdylib”, to
be discovered and built by the `cargo-build-sbf` command as a deployable program.
Solana programs also often have crate-type “rlib” so they can be linked to other Rust crates.
Avoid using “rlib” and “cdylib” crates together, since their combined usage precludes
compiler optimizations that may decrease program size and CU usage.

Prefer writing a separate package if it is supposed to be used as a library for other Solana programs (i.e. a “rlib” only crate). This would be normally the case for defining account types and helpers that are used by both clients and program. When creating a Rust project intended to be a program ready for deployment, use only the “cdylib” crate type.

[§](https://docs.rs#on-chain-vs-off-chain-compilation-targets)On-chain vs. off-chain compilation targets

Solana programs run on the [rbpf](https://github.com/solana-labs/rbpf) VM, which implements a variant of the
[eBPF](https://ebpf.io/) instruction set. Because this crate can be compiled for both on-chain
and off-chain execution, the environments of which are significantly
different, it extensively uses [conditional compilation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html) to tailor its
implementation to the environment. The `cfg` predicate used for identifying
compilation for on-chain programs is `target_os = "solana"`, as in this
example from the `solana-program` codebase that logs a message via a
syscall when run on-chain, and via a library call when offchain:

```
pub fn sol_log(message: &str) {
    #[cfg(target_os = "solana")]
    unsafe {
        sol_log_(message.as_ptr(), message.len() as u64);
    }
    #[cfg(not(target_os = "solana"))]
    program_stubs::sol_log(message);
}
```
This `cfg` pattern is suitable as well for user code that needs to work both
on-chain and off-chain.

`solana-program` and `solana-sdk` were previously a single crate. Because of
this history, and because of the dual-usage of `solana-program` for two
different environments, it contains some features that are not available to
on-chain programs at compile-time. It also contains some on-chain features
that will fail in off-chain scenarios at runtime. This distinction is not
well-reflected in the documentation.

For a more complete description of Solana’s implementation of eBPF and its
limitations, see the main Solana documentation for [on-chain programs](https://solana.com/docs/programs).

[§](https://docs.rs#core-data-types)Core data types

- `Pubkey`- [Solana account](https://solana.com/docs/core/accounts). Some account addresses are- [ed25519](https://ed25519.cr.yp.to/)public keys, with corresponding secret keys that are managed off-chain. Often, though, account addresses do not have corresponding secret keys — as with- *program derived addresses*- `Keypair`- `solana-program`but in- `solana-sdk`.
- `Hash`
- `AccountInfo`- `AccountInfo`.
- `Instruction`
- `ProgramError`- `ProgramResult`- `u64`.
- `Sol`- *lamports*- `native_token`

[§](https://docs.rs#serialization)Serialization

Within the Solana runtime, programs, and network, at least three different
serialization formats are used, and `solana-program` provides access to
those needed by programs.

In user-written Solana program code, serialization is primarily used for
accessing [ AccountInfo](https://docs.rs/sysvar/slot_history/struct.AccountInfo.html) data and

[data, both of which are program-specific binary data. Every program is free to decide their own serialization format, but data received from other sources —](https://docs.rs/instruction/struct.Instruction.html)

`Instruction`[sysvars](https://docs.rs/sysvar/index.html)for example — must be deserialized using the methods indicated by the documentation for that data or data type.

The three serialization formats in use in Solana are:

-
[Borsh](https://borsh.io/)[NEAR](https://near.org/)project, suitable for use in protocol definitions and for archival storage. It has a[Rust implementation](https://docs.rs/borsh)and a[JavaScript implementation](https://github.com/near/borsh-js)and is recommended for all purposes.Users need to import the `borsh``solana-program`, though this crate provides several useful utilities in its`borsh1`module`borsh`library.The `Instruction::new_with_borsh``Instruction`by serializing a value with borsh.
-
[Bincode](https://docs.rs/bincode)[Serde](https://serde.rs/)Rust APIs. As it does not have a specification nor a JavaScript implementation, and uses more CPU than borsh, it is not recommend for new code.Many system program and native program instructions are serialized with bincode, and it is used for other purposes in the runtime. In these cases Rust programmers are generally not directly exposed to the encoding format as it is hidden behind APIs. The `Instruction::new_with_bincode``Instruction`by serializing a value with bincode.
-
`Pack`[Solana Program Library](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana-program-library)to define their account format. It is difficult to implement and does not define a language-independent serialization format. It is not generally recommended for new code.

Developers should carefully consider the CPU cost of serialization, balanced against the need for correctness and ease of use: off-the-shelf serialization formats tend to be more expensive than carefully hand-written application-specific formats; but application-specific formats are more difficult to ensure the correctness of, and to provide multi-language implementations for. It is not uncommon for programs to pack and unpack their data with hand-written code.

[§](https://docs.rs#cross-program-instruction-execution)Cross-program instruction execution

Solana programs may call other programs, termed [ cross-program
invocation](https://docs.rs#cross-program-instruction-execution) (CPI), with the

[and](https://docs.rs/program/fn.invoke.html)

`invoke`[functions. When calling another program the caller must provide the](https://docs.rs/program/fn.invoke_signed.html)

`invoke_signed`[to be invoked, as well as the](https://docs.rs/instruction/struct.Instruction.html)

`Instruction`[for every account required by the instruction. Because the only way for a program to acquire](https://docs.rs/sysvar/slot_history/struct.AccountInfo.html)

`AccountInfo``AccountInfo` values is by receiving them from the runtime at the
[program entrypoint](https://docs.rs/macro.entrypoint.html), any account required by the callee program must transitively be required by the caller program, and provided by

*its*caller.

A simple example of transferring lamports via CPI:

```
use solana_account_info::{next_account_info, AccountInfo};
use solana_program_entrypoint::entrypoint;
use solana_program_error::ProgramResult;
use solana_cpi::invoke;
use solana_pubkey::Pubkey;
use solana_system_interface::instruction::transfer;
entrypoint!(process_instruction);
fn process_instruction(
    program_id: &Pubkey,
    accounts: &[AccountInfo],
    instruction_data: &[u8],
) -> ProgramResult {
    let account_info_iter = &mut accounts.iter();
    let payer = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    let recipient = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    assert!(payer.is_writable);
    assert!(payer.is_signer);
    assert!(recipient.is_writable);
    let lamports = 1000000;
    invoke(
        &transfer(payer.key, recipient.key, lamports),
        &[payer.clone(), recipient.clone()],
    )
}
```
Solana also includes a mechanism to let programs control and sign for
accounts without needing to protect a corresponding secret key, called
[ program derived addresses](https://solana.com/docs/core/cpi#program-derived-addresses). PDAs are derived with the

[function. With a PDA, a program can call](https://docs.rs/solana-address/1.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/solana_address/struct.Address.html#method.find_program_address)

`Pubkey::find_program_address``invoke_signed` to call another program while virtually “signing” for the
PDA.A simple example of creating an account for a PDA:

```
use solana_account_info::{next_account_info, AccountInfo};
use solana_program_entrypoint::entrypoint;
use solana_program_error::ProgramResult;
use solana_cpi::invoke_signed;
use solana_pubkey::Pubkey;
use solana_system_interface::instruction::create_account;
entrypoint!(process_instruction);
fn process_instruction(
    program_id: &Pubkey,
    accounts: &[AccountInfo],
    instruction_data: &[u8],
) -> ProgramResult {
    let account_info_iter = &mut accounts.iter();
    let payer = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    let vault_pda = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    let system_program = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    assert!(payer.is_writable);
    assert!(payer.is_signer);
    assert!(vault_pda.is_writable);
    assert_eq!(vault_pda.owner, &solana_system_interface::program::ID);
    assert!(solana_system_interface::program::check_id(system_program.key));
    let vault_bump_seed = instruction_data[0];
    let vault_seeds = &[b"vault", payer.key.as_ref(), &[vault_bump_seed]];
    let expected_vault_pda = Pubkey::create_program_address(vault_seeds, program_id)?;
    assert_eq!(vault_pda.key, &expected_vault_pda);
    let lamports = 10000000;
    let vault_size = 16;
    invoke_signed(
        &create_account(
            &payer.key,
            &vault_pda.key,
            lamports,
            vault_size,
            &program_id,
        ),
        &[
            payer.clone(),
            vault_pda.clone(),
        ],
        &[
            &[
                b"vault",
                payer.key.as_ref(),
                &[vault_bump_seed],
            ],
        ]
    )?;
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#native-programs)Native programs

Some solana programs are [ native programs](https://docs.solanalabs.com/runtime/programs), running native machine
code that is distributed with the runtime, with well-known program IDs.

Some native programs can be [invoked](https://docs.rs#cross-program-instruction-execution) by other programs, but some can
only be executed as “top-level” instructions included by off-chain clients
in a [ Transaction](https://docs.rs/solana-sdk/latest/solana_sdk/transaction/struct.Transaction.html).

This crate defines the program IDs for most native programs. Even though some native programs cannot be invoked by other programs, a Solana program may need access to their program IDs. For example, a program may need to verify that an ed25519 signature verification instruction was included in the same transaction as its own instruction. For many native programs, this crate also defines enums that represent the instructions they process, and constructors for building the instructions.

Locations of program IDs and instruction constructors are noted in the list below, as well as whether they are invokable by other programs.

While some native programs have been active since the genesis block, others
are activated dynamically after a specific [slot](https://solana.com/docs/terminology#slot), and some are not yet
active. This documentation does not distinguish which native programs are
active on any particular network. The `solana feature status` CLI command
can help in determining active features.

Native programs important to Solana program authors include:

-
**System Program**: Creates new accounts, allocates account data, assigns accounts to owning programs, transfers lamports from System Program owned accounts and pays transaction fees.- ID: `solana_system_interface::program::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_system_interface::instruction`
- Invokable by programs? yes

- ID:
-
**Compute Budget Program**: Requests additional CPU or memory resources for a transaction. This program does nothing when called from another program.- ID: `solana_compute_budget_interface::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_compute_budget_interface::ComputeBudgetInstruction`
- Invokable by programs? no

- ID:
-
**ed25519 Program**: Verifies an ed25519 signature.- ID: `solana_sdk_ids::ed25519_program::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_ed25519_program::new_ed25519_instruction_with_signature`
- Invokable by programs? no

- ID:
-
**secp256k1 Program**: Verifies secp256k1 public key recovery operations.- ID: `solana_sdk_ids::secp256k1_program::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_secp256k1_program::new_secp256k1_instruction_with_signature`
- Invokable by programs? no

- ID:
-
**BPF Loader**: Deploys, and executes immutable programs on the chain.- ID: `solana_sdk_ids::bpf_loader::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_loader_v2_interface::instruction`
- Invokable by programs? yes

- ID:
-
**Upgradable BPF Loader**: Deploys, upgrades, and executes upgradable programs on the chain.- ID: `solana_sdk_ids::bpf_loader_upgradeable::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_loader_v3_interface::instruction`
- Invokable by programs? yes

- ID:
-
**Deprecated BPF Loader**: Deploys, and executes immutable programs on the chain.- ID: `solana_sdk_ids::bpf_loader_deprecated::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_loader_v2_interface::instruction`
- Invokable by programs? yes

- ID:

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_heap_default.html)- heap_ - default
- Define the default global allocator.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_panic_default.html)- panic_ - default
- Define the default global panic handler.
- [declare_](https://docs.rs/macro.declare_deprecated_id.html)- deprecated_ - id
- Same as `declare_id`
- [declare_](https://docs.rs/macro.declare_deprecated_sysvar_id.html)- deprecated_ - sysvar_ - id
- Same as `declare_sysvar_id`
- [declare_](https://docs.rs/macro.declare_id.html)- id
- Convenience macro to declare a static address and functions to interact with it.
- [declare_](https://docs.rs/macro.declare_sysvar_id.html)- sysvar_ - id
- Declares an ID that implements `SysvarId`
- [entrypoint](https://docs.rs/macro.entrypoint.html)
- Declare the program entrypoint and set up global handlers.
- [entrypoint_](https://docs.rs/macro.entrypoint_deprecated.html)- deprecated
- Declare the program entrypoint.
- [entrypoint_](https://docs.rs/macro.entrypoint_no_alloc.html)- no_ - alloc
- Declare the program entrypoint and set up global handlers.
- [impl_](https://docs.rs/macro.impl_sysvar_get.html)- sysvar_ - get
- Implements the `Sysvar::get`
- [msg](https://docs.rs/macro.msg.html)
- Print a message to the log.
- [pubkey](https://docs.rs/macro.pubkey.html)
- Convenience macro to define a static `Address`value.
- [unchecked_](https://docs.rs/macro.unchecked_div_by_const.html)- div_ - by_ - const
- Convenience macro for doing integer division where the operation’s safety can be checked at compile-time.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Badges

Source: https://docs.rs/about/badges

Docs.rs no longer has its own badges. Consider using [shields.io](https://shields.io) instead.

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```
