# solana_program - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/solana-program/4.0.0/target-redirect/solana_program/

## Expand description

The base library for all Solana on-chain Rust programs.

All Solana Rust programs that run on-chain will link to this crate, which
acts as a standard library for Solana programs. Solana programs also link to
the [Rust standard library](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/), though it is [modified](https://solana.com/docs/programs/limitations#rust-libraries) for the
Solana runtime environment. While off-chain programs that interact with the
Solana network *can* link to this crate, they typically instead use the
[ solana-sdk](https://docs.rs/solana-sdk/latest/solana_sdk/) crate, which reexports all modules from

`solana-program`.This library defines

- macros for declaring the [program entrypoint](https://docs.rs#defining-a-solana-program),
- [core data types](https://docs.rs#core-data-types),
- [logging](https://docs.rs/log/index.html)macros,
- [serialization](https://docs.rs#serialization)methods,
- methods for [cross-program instruction execution](https://docs.rs#cross-program-instruction-execution),
- program IDs and instruction constructors for the system program and other
[native programs](https://docs.rs#native-programs),
- [sysvar](https://docs.rs/sysvar/index.html)accessors.

Idiomatic examples of `solana-program` usage can be found in
[the Solana Program Library](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana-program-library).

[§](https://docs.rs#defining-a-solana-program)Defining a solana program

Solana program crates have some unique properties compared to typical Rust programs:

- They are often compiled for both on-chain use and off-chain use. This is primarily because off-chain clients may need access to data types defined by the on-chain program.
- They do not define a `main`function, but instead define their entrypoint with the`entrypoint!`
- They are compiled as the [“cdylib”](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/linkage.html)crate type for dynamic loading by the Solana runtime.
- They run in a constrained VM environment, and while they do have access to
the [Rust standard library](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/), many features of the standard library, particularly related to OS services, will fail at runtime, will silently do nothing, or are not defined. See the[restrictions to the Rust standard library](https://solana.com/docs/programs/limitations#rust-libraries)in the Solana documentation for more.

Because multiple crates that are linked together cannot all define
program entrypoints (see the [ entrypoint!](https://docs.rs/macro.entrypoint.html) documentation) a common
convention is to use a

[Cargo feature](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/features.html)called

`no-entrypoint` to allow
the program entrypoint to be disabled.The skeleton of a Solana program typically looks like:

```
#[cfg(not(feature = "no-entrypoint"))]
pub mod entrypoint {
    use solana_program::{
        account_info::AccountInfo,
        entrypoint,
        entrypoint::ProgramResult,
        pubkey::Pubkey,
    };
    entrypoint!(process_instruction);
    pub fn process_instruction(
        program_id: &Pubkey,
        accounts: &[AccountInfo],
        instruction_data: &[u8],
    ) -> ProgramResult {
        // Decode and dispatch instructions here.
        todo!()
    }
}
// Additional code goes here.
```
With a `Cargo.toml` file that contains

```
[lib]
crate-type = ["cdylib"]
[features]
no-entrypoint = []
```
Note that a Solana program must specify its crate-type as “cdylib”, to
be discovered and built by the `cargo-build-sbf` command as a deployable program.
Solana programs also often have crate-type “rlib” so they can be linked to other Rust crates.
Avoid using “rlib” and “cdylib” crates together, since their combined usage precludes
compiler optimizations that may decrease program size and CU usage.

Prefer writing a separate package if it is supposed to be used as a library for other Solana programs (i.e. a “rlib” only crate). This would be normally the case for defining account types and helpers that are used by both clients and program. When creating a Rust project intended to be a program ready for deployment, use only the “cdylib” crate type.

[§](https://docs.rs#on-chain-vs-off-chain-compilation-targets)On-chain vs. off-chain compilation targets

Solana programs run on the [rbpf](https://github.com/solana-labs/rbpf) VM, which implements a variant of the
[eBPF](https://ebpf.io/) instruction set. Because this crate can be compiled for both on-chain
and off-chain execution, the environments of which are significantly
different, it extensively uses [conditional compilation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html) to tailor its
implementation to the environment. The `cfg` predicate used for identifying
compilation for on-chain programs is `target_os = "solana"`, as in this
example from the `solana-program` codebase that logs a message via a
syscall when run on-chain, and via a library call when offchain:

```
pub fn sol_log(message: &str) {
    #[cfg(target_os = "solana")]
    unsafe {
        sol_log_(message.as_ptr(), message.len() as u64);
    }
    #[cfg(not(target_os = "solana"))]
    program_stubs::sol_log(message);
}
```
This `cfg` pattern is suitable as well for user code that needs to work both
on-chain and off-chain.

`solana-program` and `solana-sdk` were previously a single crate. Because of
this history, and because of the dual-usage of `solana-program` for two
different environments, it contains some features that are not available to
on-chain programs at compile-time. It also contains some on-chain features
that will fail in off-chain scenarios at runtime. This distinction is not
well-reflected in the documentation.

For a more complete description of Solana’s implementation of eBPF and its
limitations, see the main Solana documentation for [on-chain programs](https://solana.com/docs/programs).

[§](https://docs.rs#core-data-types)Core data types

- `Pubkey`- [Solana account](https://solana.com/docs/core/accounts). Some account addresses are- [ed25519](https://ed25519.cr.yp.to/)public keys, with corresponding secret keys that are managed off-chain. Often, though, account addresses do not have corresponding secret keys — as with- *program derived addresses*- `Keypair`- `solana-program`but in- `solana-sdk`.
- `Hash`
- `AccountInfo`- `AccountInfo`.
- `Instruction`
- `ProgramError`- `ProgramResult`- `u64`.
- `Sol`- *lamports*- `native_token`

[§](https://docs.rs#serialization)Serialization

Within the Solana runtime, programs, and network, at least three different
serialization formats are used, and `solana-program` provides access to
those needed by programs.

In user-written Solana program code, serialization is primarily used for
accessing [ AccountInfo](https://docs.rs/sysvar/slot_history/struct.AccountInfo.html) data and

[data, both of which are program-specific binary data. Every program is free to decide their own serialization format, but data received from other sources —](https://docs.rs/instruction/struct.Instruction.html)

`Instruction`[sysvars](https://docs.rs/sysvar/index.html)for example — must be deserialized using the methods indicated by the documentation for that data or data type.

The three serialization formats in use in Solana are:

-
[Borsh](https://borsh.io/)[NEAR](https://near.org/)project, suitable for use in protocol definitions and for archival storage. It has a[Rust implementation](https://docs.rs/borsh)and a[JavaScript implementation](https://github.com/near/borsh-js)and is recommended for all purposes.Users need to import the `borsh``solana-program`, though this crate provides several useful utilities in its`borsh1`module`borsh`library.The `Instruction::new_with_borsh``Instruction`by serializing a value with borsh.
-
[Bincode](https://docs.rs/bincode)[Serde](https://serde.rs/)Rust APIs. As it does not have a specification nor a JavaScript implementation, and uses more CPU than borsh, it is not recommend for new code.Many system program and native program instructions are serialized with bincode, and it is used for other purposes in the runtime. In these cases Rust programmers are generally not directly exposed to the encoding format as it is hidden behind APIs. The `Instruction::new_with_bincode``Instruction`by serializing a value with bincode.
-
`Pack`[Solana Program Library](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana-program-library)to define their account format. It is difficult to implement and does not define a language-independent serialization format. It is not generally recommended for new code.

Developers should carefully consider the CPU cost of serialization, balanced against the need for correctness and ease of use: off-the-shelf serialization formats tend to be more expensive than carefully hand-written application-specific formats; but application-specific formats are more difficult to ensure the correctness of, and to provide multi-language implementations for. It is not uncommon for programs to pack and unpack their data with hand-written code.

[§](https://docs.rs#cross-program-instruction-execution)Cross-program instruction execution

Solana programs may call other programs, termed [ cross-program
invocation](https://docs.rs#cross-program-instruction-execution) (CPI), with the

[and](https://docs.rs/program/fn.invoke.html)

`invoke`[functions. When calling another program the caller must provide the](https://docs.rs/program/fn.invoke_signed.html)

`invoke_signed`[to be invoked, as well as the](https://docs.rs/instruction/struct.Instruction.html)

`Instruction`[for every account required by the instruction. Because the only way for a program to acquire](https://docs.rs/sysvar/slot_history/struct.AccountInfo.html)

`AccountInfo``AccountInfo` values is by receiving them from the runtime at the
[program entrypoint](https://docs.rs/macro.entrypoint.html), any account required by the callee program must transitively be required by the caller program, and provided by

*its*caller.

A simple example of transferring lamports via CPI:

```
use solana_account_info::{next_account_info, AccountInfo};
use solana_program_entrypoint::entrypoint;
use solana_program_error::ProgramResult;
use solana_cpi::invoke;
use solana_pubkey::Pubkey;
use solana_system_interface::instruction::transfer;
entrypoint!(process_instruction);
fn process_instruction(
    program_id: &Pubkey,
    accounts: &[AccountInfo],
    instruction_data: &[u8],
) -> ProgramResult {
    let account_info_iter = &mut accounts.iter();
    let payer = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    let recipient = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    assert!(payer.is_writable);
    assert!(payer.is_signer);
    assert!(recipient.is_writable);
    let lamports = 1000000;
    invoke(
        &transfer(payer.key, recipient.key, lamports),
        &[payer.clone(), recipient.clone()],
    )
}
```
Solana also includes a mechanism to let programs control and sign for
accounts without needing to protect a corresponding secret key, called
[ program derived addresses](https://solana.com/docs/core/cpi#program-derived-addresses). PDAs are derived with the

[function. With a PDA, a program can call](https://docs.rs/solana-address/1.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/solana_address/struct.Address.html#method.find_program_address)

`Pubkey::find_program_address``invoke_signed` to call another program while virtually “signing” for the
PDA.A simple example of creating an account for a PDA:

```
use solana_account_info::{next_account_info, AccountInfo};
use solana_program_entrypoint::entrypoint;
use solana_program_error::ProgramResult;
use solana_cpi::invoke_signed;
use solana_pubkey::Pubkey;
use solana_system_interface::instruction::create_account;
entrypoint!(process_instruction);
fn process_instruction(
    program_id: &Pubkey,
    accounts: &[AccountInfo],
    instruction_data: &[u8],
) -> ProgramResult {
    let account_info_iter = &mut accounts.iter();
    let payer = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    let vault_pda = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    let system_program = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    assert!(payer.is_writable);
    assert!(payer.is_signer);
    assert!(vault_pda.is_writable);
    assert_eq!(vault_pda.owner, &solana_system_interface::program::ID);
    assert!(solana_system_interface::program::check_id(system_program.key));
    let vault_bump_seed = instruction_data[0];
    let vault_seeds = &[b"vault", payer.key.as_ref(), &[vault_bump_seed]];
    let expected_vault_pda = Pubkey::create_program_address(vault_seeds, program_id)?;
    assert_eq!(vault_pda.key, &expected_vault_pda);
    let lamports = 10000000;
    let vault_size = 16;
    invoke_signed(
        &create_account(
            &payer.key,
            &vault_pda.key,
            lamports,
            vault_size,
            &program_id,
        ),
        &[
            payer.clone(),
            vault_pda.clone(),
        ],
        &[
            &[
                b"vault",
                payer.key.as_ref(),
                &[vault_bump_seed],
            ],
        ]
    )?;
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#native-programs)Native programs

Some solana programs are [ native programs](https://docs.solanalabs.com/runtime/programs), running native machine
code that is distributed with the runtime, with well-known program IDs.

Some native programs can be [invoked](https://docs.rs#cross-program-instruction-execution) by other programs, but some can
only be executed as “top-level” instructions included by off-chain clients
in a [ Transaction](https://docs.rs/solana-sdk/latest/solana_sdk/transaction/struct.Transaction.html).

This crate defines the program IDs for most native programs. Even though some native programs cannot be invoked by other programs, a Solana program may need access to their program IDs. For example, a program may need to verify that an ed25519 signature verification instruction was included in the same transaction as its own instruction. For many native programs, this crate also defines enums that represent the instructions they process, and constructors for building the instructions.

Locations of program IDs and instruction constructors are noted in the list below, as well as whether they are invokable by other programs.

While some native programs have been active since the genesis block, others
are activated dynamically after a specific [slot](https://solana.com/docs/terminology#slot), and some are not yet
active. This documentation does not distinguish which native programs are
active on any particular network. The `solana feature status` CLI command
can help in determining active features.

Native programs important to Solana program authors include:

-
**System Program**: Creates new accounts, allocates account data, assigns accounts to owning programs, transfers lamports from System Program owned accounts and pays transaction fees.- ID: `solana_system_interface::program::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_system_interface::instruction`
- Invokable by programs? yes

- ID:
-
**Compute Budget Program**: Requests additional CPU or memory resources for a transaction. This program does nothing when called from another program.- ID: `solana_compute_budget_interface::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_compute_budget_interface::ComputeBudgetInstruction`
- Invokable by programs? no

- ID:
-
**ed25519 Program**: Verifies an ed25519 signature.- ID: `solana_sdk_ids::ed25519_program::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_ed25519_program::new_ed25519_instruction_with_signature`
- Invokable by programs? no

- ID:
-
**secp256k1 Program**: Verifies secp256k1 public key recovery operations.- ID: `solana_sdk_ids::secp256k1_program::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_secp256k1_program::new_secp256k1_instruction_with_signature`
- Invokable by programs? no

- ID:
-
**BPF Loader**: Deploys, and executes immutable programs on the chain.- ID: `solana_sdk_ids::bpf_loader::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_loader_v2_interface::instruction`
- Invokable by programs? yes

- ID:
-
**Upgradable BPF Loader**: Deploys, upgrades, and executes upgradable programs on the chain.- ID: `solana_sdk_ids::bpf_loader_upgradeable::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_loader_v3_interface::instruction`
- Invokable by programs? yes

- ID:
-
**Deprecated BPF Loader**: Deploys, and executes immutable programs on the chain.- ID: `solana_sdk_ids::bpf_loader_deprecated::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_loader_v2_interface::instruction`
- Invokable by programs? yes

- ID:

# solana_program - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-program/4.0.0/solana_program/index.html

## Expand description

The base library for all Solana on-chain Rust programs.

All Solana Rust programs that run on-chain will link to this crate, which
acts as a standard library for Solana programs. Solana programs also link to
the [Rust standard library](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/), though it is [modified](https://solana.com/docs/programs/limitations#rust-libraries) for the
Solana runtime environment. While off-chain programs that interact with the
Solana network *can* link to this crate, they typically instead use the
[ solana-sdk](https://docs.rs/solana-sdk/latest/solana_sdk/) crate, which reexports all modules from

`solana-program`.This library defines

- macros for declaring the [program entrypoint](https://docs.rs#defining-a-solana-program),
- [core data types](https://docs.rs#core-data-types),
- [logging](https://docs.rs/log/index.html)macros,
- [serialization](https://docs.rs#serialization)methods,
- methods for [cross-program instruction execution](https://docs.rs#cross-program-instruction-execution),
- program IDs and instruction constructors for the system program and other
[native programs](https://docs.rs#native-programs),
- [sysvar](https://docs.rs/sysvar/index.html)accessors.

Idiomatic examples of `solana-program` usage can be found in
[the Solana Program Library](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana-program-library).

[§](https://docs.rs#defining-a-solana-program)Defining a solana program

Solana program crates have some unique properties compared to typical Rust programs:

- They are often compiled for both on-chain use and off-chain use. This is primarily because off-chain clients may need access to data types defined by the on-chain program.
- They do not define a `main`function, but instead define their entrypoint with the`entrypoint!`
- They are compiled as the [“cdylib”](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/linkage.html)crate type for dynamic loading by the Solana runtime.
- They run in a constrained VM environment, and while they do have access to
the [Rust standard library](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/), many features of the standard library, particularly related to OS services, will fail at runtime, will silently do nothing, or are not defined. See the[restrictions to the Rust standard library](https://solana.com/docs/programs/limitations#rust-libraries)in the Solana documentation for more.

Because multiple crates that are linked together cannot all define
program entrypoints (see the [ entrypoint!](https://docs.rs/macro.entrypoint.html) documentation) a common
convention is to use a

[Cargo feature](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/features.html)called

`no-entrypoint` to allow
the program entrypoint to be disabled.The skeleton of a Solana program typically looks like:

```
#[cfg(not(feature = "no-entrypoint"))]
pub mod entrypoint {
    use solana_program::{
        account_info::AccountInfo,
        entrypoint,
        entrypoint::ProgramResult,
        pubkey::Pubkey,
    };
    entrypoint!(process_instruction);
    pub fn process_instruction(
        program_id: &Pubkey,
        accounts: &[AccountInfo],
        instruction_data: &[u8],
    ) -> ProgramResult {
        // Decode and dispatch instructions here.
        todo!()
    }
}
// Additional code goes here.
```
With a `Cargo.toml` file that contains

```
[lib]
crate-type = ["cdylib"]
[features]
no-entrypoint = []
```
Note that a Solana program must specify its crate-type as “cdylib”, to
be discovered and built by the `cargo-build-sbf` command as a deployable program.
Solana programs also often have crate-type “rlib” so they can be linked to other Rust crates.
Avoid using “rlib” and “cdylib” crates together, since their combined usage precludes
compiler optimizations that may decrease program size and CU usage.

Prefer writing a separate package if it is supposed to be used as a library for other Solana programs (i.e. a “rlib” only crate). This would be normally the case for defining account types and helpers that are used by both clients and program. When creating a Rust project intended to be a program ready for deployment, use only the “cdylib” crate type.

[§](https://docs.rs#on-chain-vs-off-chain-compilation-targets)On-chain vs. off-chain compilation targets

Solana programs run on the [rbpf](https://github.com/solana-labs/rbpf) VM, which implements a variant of the
[eBPF](https://ebpf.io/) instruction set. Because this crate can be compiled for both on-chain
and off-chain execution, the environments of which are significantly
different, it extensively uses [conditional compilation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html) to tailor its
implementation to the environment. The `cfg` predicate used for identifying
compilation for on-chain programs is `target_os = "solana"`, as in this
example from the `solana-program` codebase that logs a message via a
syscall when run on-chain, and via a library call when offchain:

```
pub fn sol_log(message: &str) {
    #[cfg(target_os = "solana")]
    unsafe {
        sol_log_(message.as_ptr(), message.len() as u64);
    }
    #[cfg(not(target_os = "solana"))]
    program_stubs::sol_log(message);
}
```
This `cfg` pattern is suitable as well for user code that needs to work both
on-chain and off-chain.

`solana-program` and `solana-sdk` were previously a single crate. Because of
this history, and because of the dual-usage of `solana-program` for two
different environments, it contains some features that are not available to
on-chain programs at compile-time. It also contains some on-chain features
that will fail in off-chain scenarios at runtime. This distinction is not
well-reflected in the documentation.

For a more complete description of Solana’s implementation of eBPF and its
limitations, see the main Solana documentation for [on-chain programs](https://solana.com/docs/programs).

[§](https://docs.rs#core-data-types)Core data types

- `Pubkey`- [Solana account](https://solana.com/docs/core/accounts). Some account addresses are- [ed25519](https://ed25519.cr.yp.to/)public keys, with corresponding secret keys that are managed off-chain. Often, though, account addresses do not have corresponding secret keys — as with- *program derived addresses*- `Keypair`- `solana-program`but in- `solana-sdk`.
- `Hash`
- `AccountInfo`- `AccountInfo`.
- `Instruction`
- `ProgramError`- `ProgramResult`- `u64`.
- `Sol`- *lamports*- `native_token`

[§](https://docs.rs#serialization)Serialization

Within the Solana runtime, programs, and network, at least three different
serialization formats are used, and `solana-program` provides access to
those needed by programs.

In user-written Solana program code, serialization is primarily used for
accessing [ AccountInfo](https://docs.rs/sysvar/slot_history/struct.AccountInfo.html) data and

[data, both of which are program-specific binary data. Every program is free to decide their own serialization format, but data received from other sources —](https://docs.rs/instruction/struct.Instruction.html)

`Instruction`[sysvars](https://docs.rs/sysvar/index.html)for example — must be deserialized using the methods indicated by the documentation for that data or data type.

The three serialization formats in use in Solana are:

-
[Borsh](https://borsh.io/)[NEAR](https://near.org/)project, suitable for use in protocol definitions and for archival storage. It has a[Rust implementation](https://docs.rs/borsh)and a[JavaScript implementation](https://github.com/near/borsh-js)and is recommended for all purposes.Users need to import the `borsh``solana-program`, though this crate provides several useful utilities in its`borsh1`module`borsh`library.The `Instruction::new_with_borsh``Instruction`by serializing a value with borsh.
-
[Bincode](https://docs.rs/bincode)[Serde](https://serde.rs/)Rust APIs. As it does not have a specification nor a JavaScript implementation, and uses more CPU than borsh, it is not recommend for new code.Many system program and native program instructions are serialized with bincode, and it is used for other purposes in the runtime. In these cases Rust programmers are generally not directly exposed to the encoding format as it is hidden behind APIs. The `Instruction::new_with_bincode``Instruction`by serializing a value with bincode.
-
`Pack`[Solana Program Library](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana-program-library)to define their account format. It is difficult to implement and does not define a language-independent serialization format. It is not generally recommended for new code.

Developers should carefully consider the CPU cost of serialization, balanced against the need for correctness and ease of use: off-the-shelf serialization formats tend to be more expensive than carefully hand-written application-specific formats; but application-specific formats are more difficult to ensure the correctness of, and to provide multi-language implementations for. It is not uncommon for programs to pack and unpack their data with hand-written code.

[§](https://docs.rs#cross-program-instruction-execution)Cross-program instruction execution

Solana programs may call other programs, termed [ cross-program
invocation](https://docs.rs#cross-program-instruction-execution) (CPI), with the

[and](https://docs.rs/program/fn.invoke.html)

`invoke`[functions. When calling another program the caller must provide the](https://docs.rs/program/fn.invoke_signed.html)

`invoke_signed`[to be invoked, as well as the](https://docs.rs/instruction/struct.Instruction.html)

`Instruction`[for every account required by the instruction. Because the only way for a program to acquire](https://docs.rs/sysvar/slot_history/struct.AccountInfo.html)

`AccountInfo``AccountInfo` values is by receiving them from the runtime at the
[program entrypoint](https://docs.rs/macro.entrypoint.html), any account required by the callee program must transitively be required by the caller program, and provided by

*its*caller.

A simple example of transferring lamports via CPI:

```
use solana_account_info::{next_account_info, AccountInfo};
use solana_program_entrypoint::entrypoint;
use solana_program_error::ProgramResult;
use solana_cpi::invoke;
use solana_pubkey::Pubkey;
use solana_system_interface::instruction::transfer;
entrypoint!(process_instruction);
fn process_instruction(
    program_id: &Pubkey,
    accounts: &[AccountInfo],
    instruction_data: &[u8],
) -> ProgramResult {
    let account_info_iter = &mut accounts.iter();
    let payer = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    let recipient = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    assert!(payer.is_writable);
    assert!(payer.is_signer);
    assert!(recipient.is_writable);
    let lamports = 1000000;
    invoke(
        &transfer(payer.key, recipient.key, lamports),
        &[payer.clone(), recipient.clone()],
    )
}
```
Solana also includes a mechanism to let programs control and sign for
accounts without needing to protect a corresponding secret key, called
[ program derived addresses](https://solana.com/docs/core/cpi#program-derived-addresses). PDAs are derived with the

[function. With a PDA, a program can call](https://docs.rs/solana-address/1.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/solana_address/struct.Address.html#method.find_program_address)

`Pubkey::find_program_address``invoke_signed` to call another program while virtually “signing” for the
PDA.A simple example of creating an account for a PDA:

```
use solana_account_info::{next_account_info, AccountInfo};
use solana_program_entrypoint::entrypoint;
use solana_program_error::ProgramResult;
use solana_cpi::invoke_signed;
use solana_pubkey::Pubkey;
use solana_system_interface::instruction::create_account;
entrypoint!(process_instruction);
fn process_instruction(
    program_id: &Pubkey,
    accounts: &[AccountInfo],
    instruction_data: &[u8],
) -> ProgramResult {
    let account_info_iter = &mut accounts.iter();
    let payer = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    let vault_pda = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    let system_program = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    assert!(payer.is_writable);
    assert!(payer.is_signer);
    assert!(vault_pda.is_writable);
    assert_eq!(vault_pda.owner, &solana_system_interface::program::ID);
    assert!(solana_system_interface::program::check_id(system_program.key));
    let vault_bump_seed = instruction_data[0];
    let vault_seeds = &[b"vault", payer.key.as_ref(), &[vault_bump_seed]];
    let expected_vault_pda = Pubkey::create_program_address(vault_seeds, program_id)?;
    assert_eq!(vault_pda.key, &expected_vault_pda);
    let lamports = 10000000;
    let vault_size = 16;
    invoke_signed(
        &create_account(
            &payer.key,
            &vault_pda.key,
            lamports,
            vault_size,
            &program_id,
        ),
        &[
            payer.clone(),
            vault_pda.clone(),
        ],
        &[
            &[
                b"vault",
                payer.key.as_ref(),
                &[vault_bump_seed],
            ],
        ]
    )?;
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#native-programs)Native programs

Some solana programs are [ native programs](https://docs.solanalabs.com/runtime/programs), running native machine
code that is distributed with the runtime, with well-known program IDs.

Some native programs can be [invoked](https://docs.rs#cross-program-instruction-execution) by other programs, but some can
only be executed as “top-level” instructions included by off-chain clients
in a [ Transaction](https://docs.rs/solana-sdk/latest/solana_sdk/transaction/struct.Transaction.html).

This crate defines the program IDs for most native programs. Even though some native programs cannot be invoked by other programs, a Solana program may need access to their program IDs. For example, a program may need to verify that an ed25519 signature verification instruction was included in the same transaction as its own instruction. For many native programs, this crate also defines enums that represent the instructions they process, and constructors for building the instructions.

Locations of program IDs and instruction constructors are noted in the list below, as well as whether they are invokable by other programs.

While some native programs have been active since the genesis block, others
are activated dynamically after a specific [slot](https://solana.com/docs/terminology#slot), and some are not yet
active. This documentation does not distinguish which native programs are
active on any particular network. The `solana feature status` CLI command
can help in determining active features.

Native programs important to Solana program authors include:

-
**System Program**: Creates new accounts, allocates account data, assigns accounts to owning programs, transfers lamports from System Program owned accounts and pays transaction fees.- ID: `solana_system_interface::program::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_system_interface::instruction`
- Invokable by programs? yes

- ID:
-
**Compute Budget Program**: Requests additional CPU or memory resources for a transaction. This program does nothing when called from another program.- ID: `solana_compute_budget_interface::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_compute_budget_interface::ComputeBudgetInstruction`
- Invokable by programs? no

- ID:
-
**ed25519 Program**: Verifies an ed25519 signature.- ID: `solana_sdk_ids::ed25519_program::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_ed25519_program::new_ed25519_instruction_with_signature`
- Invokable by programs? no

- ID:
-
**secp256k1 Program**: Verifies secp256k1 public key recovery operations.- ID: `solana_sdk_ids::secp256k1_program::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_secp256k1_program::new_secp256k1_instruction_with_signature`
- Invokable by programs? no

- ID:
-
**BPF Loader**: Deploys, and executes immutable programs on the chain.- ID: `solana_sdk_ids::bpf_loader::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_loader_v2_interface::instruction`
- Invokable by programs? yes

- ID:
-
**Upgradable BPF Loader**: Deploys, upgrades, and executes upgradable programs on the chain.- ID: `solana_sdk_ids::bpf_loader_upgradeable::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_loader_v3_interface::instruction`
- Invokable by programs? yes

- ID:
-
**Deprecated BPF Loader**: Deploys, and executes immutable programs on the chain.- ID: `solana_sdk_ids::bpf_loader_deprecated::ID`
- Instruction: `solana_loader_v2_interface::instruction`
- Invokable by programs? yes

- ID:

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-program/4.0.0/src/solana_program/lib.rs.html

# solana_program/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! The base library for all Solana on-chain Rust programs.
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! All Solana Rust programs that run on-chain will link to this crate, which
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! acts as a standard library for Solana programs. Solana programs also link to
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! the [Rust standard library][std], though it is [modified][sstd] for the
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! Solana runtime environment. While off-chain programs that interact with the
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! Solana network _can_ link to this crate, they typically instead use the
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! [`solana-sdk`] crate, which reexports all modules from `solana-program`.
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//!
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! [std]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! [sstd]: https://solana.com/docs/programs/limitations#rust-libraries
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! [`solana-sdk`]: https://docs.rs/solana-sdk/latest/solana_sdk/
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! This library defines
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//!
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! - macros for declaring the [program entrypoint][pe],
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! - [core data types][cdt],
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! - [logging] macros,
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! - [serialization] methods,
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! - methods for [cross-program instruction execution][cpi],
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! - program IDs and instruction constructors for the system program and other
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!   [native programs][np],
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! - [sysvar] accessors.
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! [pe]: #defining-a-solana-program
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! [cdt]: #core-data-types
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! [logging]: crate::log
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! [serialization]: #serialization
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! [np]: #native-programs
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! [cpi]: #cross-program-instruction-execution
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! [sysvar]: crate::sysvar
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! Idiomatic examples of `solana-program` usage can be found in
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! [the Solana Program Library][spl].
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//!
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! [spl]: https://github.com/solana-labs/solana-program-library
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! # Defining a solana program
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! Solana program crates have some unique properties compared to typical Rust
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! programs:
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! - They are often compiled for both on-chain use and off-chain use. This is
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!   primarily because off-chain clients may need access to data types
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!   defined by the on-chain program.
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! - They do not define a `main` function, but instead define their entrypoint
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!   with the [`entrypoint!`] macro.
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! - They are compiled as the ["cdylib"] crate type for dynamic loading
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!   by the Solana runtime.
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! - They run in a constrained VM environment, and while they do have access to
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!   the [Rust standard library][std], many features of the standard library,
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!   particularly related to OS services, will fail at runtime, will silently
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!   do nothing, or are not defined. See the [restrictions to the Rust standard
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!   library][sstd] in the Solana documentation for more.
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//!
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! [std]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/index.html
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! ["cdylib"]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/linkage.html
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! Because multiple crates that are linked together cannot all define
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! program entrypoints (see the [`entrypoint!`] documentation) a common
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! convention is to use a [Cargo feature] called `no-entrypoint` to allow
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! the program entrypoint to be disabled.
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//!
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! [Cargo feature]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/features.html
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! The skeleton of a Solana program typically looks like:
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//!
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! ```
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! #[cfg(not(feature = "no-entrypoint"))]
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! pub mod entrypoint {
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//!     use solana_program::{
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//!         account_info::AccountInfo,
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!         entrypoint,
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!         entrypoint::ProgramResult,
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//!         pubkey::Pubkey,
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//!     };
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!     entrypoint!(process_instruction);
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//!     pub fn process_instruction(
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!         program_id: &Pubkey,
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//!         accounts: &[AccountInfo],
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//!         instruction_data: &[u8],
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//!     ) -> ProgramResult {
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//!         // Decode and dispatch instructions here.
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//!         todo!()
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!     }
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! }
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//!
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! // Additional code goes here.
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! ```
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//!
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! With a `Cargo.toml` file that contains
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! ```toml
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! [lib]
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! crate-type = ["cdylib"]
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//!
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! [features]
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! no-entrypoint = []
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! ```
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//!
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! Note that a Solana program must specify its crate-type as "cdylib", to
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! be discovered and built by the `cargo-build-sbf` command as a deployable program.
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! Solana programs also often have crate-type "rlib" so they can be linked to other Rust crates.
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! Avoid using "rlib" and "cdylib" crates together, since their combined usage precludes
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! compiler optimizations that may decrease program size and CU usage.
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//!
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! Prefer writing a separate package if it is supposed to be used as a library for other Solana
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! programs (i.e. a "rlib" only crate). This would be normally the case for defining account
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! types and helpers that are used by both clients and program. When creating a Rust project
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! intended to be a program ready for deployment, use only the "cdylib" crate type.
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//!
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! # On-chain vs. off-chain compilation targets
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//!
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! Solana programs run on the [rbpf] VM, which implements a variant of the
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! [eBPF] instruction set. Because this crate can be compiled for both on-chain
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! and off-chain execution, the environments of which are significantly
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! different, it extensively uses [conditional compilation][cc] to tailor its
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! implementation to the environment. The `cfg` predicate used for identifying
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! compilation for on-chain programs is `target_os = "solana"`, as in this
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//! example from the `solana-program` codebase that logs a message via a
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! syscall when run on-chain, and via a library call when offchain:
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//!
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! [rbpf]: https://github.com/solana-labs/rbpf
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! [eBPF]: https://ebpf.io/
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//! [cc]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//!
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//! ```
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! pub fn sol_log(message: &str) {
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!     #[cfg(target_os = "solana")]
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//!     unsafe {
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//!         sol_log_(message.as_ptr(), message.len() as u64);
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//!     }
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//!
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//!     #[cfg(not(target_os = "solana"))]
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//!     program_stubs::sol_log(message);
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! }
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! # mod program_stubs {
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! #     pub(crate) fn sol_log(message: &str) { }
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! # }
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! ```
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//!
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//! This `cfg` pattern is suitable as well for user code that needs to work both
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//! on-chain and off-chain.
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//!
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//! `solana-program` and `solana-sdk` were previously a single crate. Because of
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! this history, and because of the dual-usage of `solana-program` for two
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! different environments, it contains some features that are not available to
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//! on-chain programs at compile-time. It also contains some on-chain features
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! that will fail in off-chain scenarios at runtime. This distinction is not
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//! well-reflected in the documentation.
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//!
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//! For a more complete description of Solana's implementation of eBPF and its
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//! limitations, see the main Solana documentation for [on-chain programs][ocp].
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//!
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! [ocp]: https://solana.com/docs/programs
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//!
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//! # Core data types
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//!
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//! - [`Pubkey`] — The address of a [Solana account][acc]. Some account
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//!   addresses are [ed25519] public keys, with corresponding secret keys that
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//!   are managed off-chain. Often, though, account addresses do not have
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//!   corresponding secret keys — as with [_program derived
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//!   addresses_][pdas] — or the secret key is not relevant to the
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//!   operation of a program, and may have even been disposed of. As running
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//!   Solana programs can not safely create or manage secret keys, the full
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//!   [`Keypair`] is not defined in `solana-program` but in `solana-sdk`.
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//! - [`Hash`] — A cryptographic hash. Used to uniquely identify blocks,
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//!   and also for general purpose hashing.
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! - [`AccountInfo`] — A description of a single Solana account. All accounts
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//!   that might be accessed by a program invocation are provided to the program
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//!   entrypoint as `AccountInfo`.
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//! - [`Instruction`] — A directive telling the runtime to execute a program,
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//!   passing it a set of accounts and program-specific data.
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//! - [`ProgramError`] and [`ProgramResult`] — The error type that all programs
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//!   must return, reported to the runtime as a `u64`.
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//! - [`Sol`] — The Solana native token type, with conversions to and from
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//!   [_lamports_], the smallest fractional unit of SOL, in the [`native_token`]
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//!   module.
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//!
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//! [acc]: https://solana.com/docs/core/accounts
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//! [`Pubkey`]: pubkey::Pubkey
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//! [`Hash`]: hash::Hash
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//! [`Instruction`]: instruction::Instruction
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//! [`AccountInfo`]: account_info::AccountInfo
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//! [`ProgramError`]: program_error::ProgramError
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//! [`ProgramResult`]: entrypoint::ProgramResult
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//! [ed25519]: https://ed25519.cr.yp.to/
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//! [`Keypair`]: https://docs.rs/solana-sdk/latest/solana_sdk/signer/keypair/struct.Keypair.html
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//! [SHA-256]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SHA-2
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//! [`Sol`]: native_token::Sol
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//! [_lamports_]: https://solana.com/docs/intro#what-are-sols
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//!
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//! # Serialization
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//!
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//! Within the Solana runtime, programs, and network, at least three different
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//! serialization formats are used, and `solana-program` provides access to
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//! those needed by programs.
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//!
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//! In user-written Solana program code, serialization is primarily used for
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//! accessing [`AccountInfo`] data and [`Instruction`] data, both of which are
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//! program-specific binary data. Every program is free to decide their own
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//! serialization format, but data received from other sources —
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//! [sysvars][sysvar] for example — must be deserialized using the methods
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//! indicated by the documentation for that data or data type.
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//!
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//! [`AccountInfo`]: account_info::AccountInfo
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//! [`Instruction`]: instruction::Instruction
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//!
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//! The three serialization formats in use in Solana are:
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//!
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! - __[Borsh]__, a compact and well-specified format developed by the [NEAR]
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//!   project, suitable for use in protocol definitions and for archival storage.
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//!   It has a [Rust implementation][brust] and a [JavaScript implementation][bjs]
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//!   and is recommended for all purposes.
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//!
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//!   Users need to import the [`borsh`] crate themselves — it is not
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//!   re-exported by `solana-program`, though this crate provides several useful
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//!   utilities in its [`borsh1` module][borshmod] that are not available in the
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//!   `borsh` library.
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//!
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//!   The [`Instruction::new_with_borsh`] function creates an `Instruction` by
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//!   serializing a value with borsh.
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//!
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//!   [Borsh]: https://borsh.io/
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//!   [NEAR]: https://near.org/
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//!   [brust]: https://docs.rs/borsh
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//!   [bjs]: https://github.com/near/borsh-js
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//!   [`borsh`]: https://docs.rs/borsh
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//!   [borshmod]: crate::borsh1
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//!   [`Instruction::new_with_borsh`]: instruction::Instruction::new_with_borsh
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//!
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//! - __[Bincode]__, a compact serialization format that implements the [Serde]
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//!   Rust APIs. As it does not have a specification nor a JavaScript
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//!   implementation, and uses more CPU than borsh, it is not recommend for new
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//!   code.
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//!
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//!   Many system program and native program instructions are serialized with
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//!   bincode, and it is used for other purposes in the runtime. In these cases
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//!   Rust programmers are generally not directly exposed to the encoding format
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//!   as it is hidden behind APIs.
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//!
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//!   The [`Instruction::new_with_bincode`] function creates an `Instruction` by
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//!   serializing a value with bincode.
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//!
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//!   [Bincode]: https://docs.rs/bincode
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//!   [Serde]: https://serde.rs/
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//!   [`Instruction::new_with_bincode`]: instruction::Instruction::new_with_bincode
[250](https://docs.rs#250)//!
[251](https://docs.rs#251)//! - __[`Pack`]__, a Solana-specific serialization API that is used by many
[252](https://docs.rs#252)//!   older programs in the [Solana Program Library][spl] to define their
[253](https://docs.rs#253)//!   account format. It is difficult to implement and does not define a
[254](https://docs.rs#254)//!   language-independent serialization format. It is not generally recommended
[255](https://docs.rs#255)//!   for new code.
[256](https://docs.rs#256)//!
[257](https://docs.rs#257)//!   [`Pack`]: https://docs.rs/solana-program-pack/latest/trait.Pack.html
[258](https://docs.rs#258)//!
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//! Developers should carefully consider the CPU cost of serialization, balanced
[260](https://docs.rs#260)//! against the need for correctness and ease of use: off-the-shelf
[261](https://docs.rs#261)//! serialization formats tend to be more expensive than carefully hand-written
[262](https://docs.rs#262)//! application-specific formats; but application-specific formats are more
[263](https://docs.rs#263)//! difficult to ensure the correctness of, and to provide multi-language
[264](https://docs.rs#264)//! implementations for. It is not uncommon for programs to pack and unpack
[265](https://docs.rs#265)//! their data with hand-written code.
[266](https://docs.rs#266)//!
[267](https://docs.rs#267)//! # Cross-program instruction execution
[268](https://docs.rs#268)//!
[269](https://docs.rs#269)//! Solana programs may call other programs, termed [_cross-program
[270](https://docs.rs#270)//! invocation_][cpi] (CPI), with the [`invoke`] and [`invoke_signed`]
[271](https://docs.rs#271)//! functions. When calling another program the caller must provide the
[272](https://docs.rs#272)//! [`Instruction`] to be invoked, as well as the [`AccountInfo`] for every
[273](https://docs.rs#273)//! account required by the instruction. Because the only way for a program to
[274](https://docs.rs#274)//! acquire `AccountInfo` values is by receiving them from the runtime at the
[275](https://docs.rs#275)//! [program entrypoint][entrypoint!], any account required by the callee
[276](https://docs.rs#276)//! program must transitively be required by the caller program, and provided by
[277](https://docs.rs#277)//! _its_ caller.
[278](https://docs.rs#278)//!
[279](https://docs.rs#279)//! [`invoke`]: program::invoke
[280](https://docs.rs#280)//! [`invoke_signed`]: program::invoke_signed
[281](https://docs.rs#281)//! [cpi]: https://solana.com/docs/core/cpi
[282](https://docs.rs#282)//!
[283](https://docs.rs#283)//! A simple example of transferring lamports via CPI:
[284](https://docs.rs#284)//!
[285](https://docs.rs#285)//! ```
[286](https://docs.rs#286)//! use solana_account_info::{next_account_info, AccountInfo};
[287](https://docs.rs#287)//! use solana_program_entrypoint::entrypoint;
[288](https://docs.rs#288)//! use solana_program_error::ProgramResult;
[289](https://docs.rs#289)//! use solana_cpi::invoke;
[290](https://docs.rs#290)//! use solana_pubkey::Pubkey;
[291](https://docs.rs#291)//! use solana_system_interface::instruction::transfer;
[292](https://docs.rs#292)//!
[293](https://docs.rs#293)//! entrypoint!(process_instruction);
[294](https://docs.rs#294)//!
[295](https://docs.rs#295)//! fn process_instruction(
[296](https://docs.rs#296)//!     program_id: &Pubkey,
[297](https://docs.rs#297)//!     accounts: &[AccountInfo],
[298](https://docs.rs#298)//!     instruction_data: &[u8],
[299](https://docs.rs#299)//! ) -> ProgramResult {
[300](https://docs.rs#300)//!     let account_info_iter = &mut accounts.iter();
[301](https://docs.rs#301)//!
[302](https://docs.rs#302)//!     let payer = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
[303](https://docs.rs#303)//!     let recipient = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
[304](https://docs.rs#304)//!
[305](https://docs.rs#305)//!     assert!(payer.is_writable);
[306](https://docs.rs#306)//!     assert!(payer.is_signer);
[307](https://docs.rs#307)//!     assert!(recipient.is_writable);
[308](https://docs.rs#308)//!
[309](https://docs.rs#309)//!     let lamports = 1000000;
[310](https://docs.rs#310)//!
[311](https://docs.rs#311)//!     invoke(
[312](https://docs.rs#312)//!         &transfer(payer.key, recipient.key, lamports),
[313](https://docs.rs#313)//!         &[payer.clone(), recipient.clone()],
[314](https://docs.rs#314)//!     )
[315](https://docs.rs#315)//! }
[316](https://docs.rs#316)//! ```
[317](https://docs.rs#317)//!
[318](https://docs.rs#318)//! Solana also includes a mechanism to let programs control and sign for
[319](https://docs.rs#319)//! accounts without needing to protect a corresponding secret key, called
[320](https://docs.rs#320)//! [_program derived addresses_][pdas]. PDAs are derived with the
[321](https://docs.rs#321)//! [`Pubkey::find_program_address`] function. With a PDA, a program can call
[322](https://docs.rs#322)//! `invoke_signed` to call another program while virtually "signing" for the
[323](https://docs.rs#323)//! PDA.
[324](https://docs.rs#324)//!
[325](https://docs.rs#325)//! [pdas]: https://solana.com/docs/core/cpi#program-derived-addresses
[326](https://docs.rs#326)//! [`Pubkey::find_program_address`]: pubkey::Pubkey::find_program_address
[327](https://docs.rs#327)//!
[328](https://docs.rs#328)//! A simple example of creating an account for a PDA:
[329](https://docs.rs#329)//!
[330](https://docs.rs#330)//! ```
[331](https://docs.rs#331)//! use solana_account_info::{next_account_info, AccountInfo};
[332](https://docs.rs#332)//! use solana_program_entrypoint::entrypoint;
[333](https://docs.rs#333)//! use solana_program_error::ProgramResult;
[334](https://docs.rs#334)//! use solana_cpi::invoke_signed;
[335](https://docs.rs#335)//! use solana_pubkey::Pubkey;
[336](https://docs.rs#336)//! use solana_system_interface::instruction::create_account;
[337](https://docs.rs#337)//!
[338](https://docs.rs#338)//! entrypoint!(process_instruction);
[339](https://docs.rs#339)//!
[340](https://docs.rs#340)//! fn process_instruction(
[341](https://docs.rs#341)//!     program_id: &Pubkey,
[342](https://docs.rs#342)//!     accounts: &[AccountInfo],
[343](https://docs.rs#343)//!     instruction_data: &[u8],
[344](https://docs.rs#344)//! ) -> ProgramResult {
[345](https://docs.rs#345)//!     let account_info_iter = &mut accounts.iter();
[346](https://docs.rs#346)//!     let payer = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
[347](https://docs.rs#347)//!     let vault_pda = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
[348](https://docs.rs#348)//!     let system_program = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
[349](https://docs.rs#349)//!
[350](https://docs.rs#350)//!     assert!(payer.is_writable);
[351](https://docs.rs#351)//!     assert!(payer.is_signer);
[352](https://docs.rs#352)//!     assert!(vault_pda.is_writable);
[353](https://docs.rs#353)//!     assert_eq!(vault_pda.owner, &solana_system_interface::program::ID);
[354](https://docs.rs#354)//!     assert!(solana_system_interface::program::check_id(system_program.key));
[355](https://docs.rs#355)//!
[356](https://docs.rs#356)//!     let vault_bump_seed = instruction_data[0];
[357](https://docs.rs#357)//!     let vault_seeds = &[b"vault", payer.key.as_ref(), &[vault_bump_seed]];
[358](https://docs.rs#358)//!     let expected_vault_pda = Pubkey::create_program_address(vault_seeds, program_id)?;
[359](https://docs.rs#359)//!
[360](https://docs.rs#360)//!     assert_eq!(vault_pda.key, &expected_vault_pda);
[361](https://docs.rs#361)//!
[362](https://docs.rs#362)//!     let lamports = 10000000;
[363](https://docs.rs#363)//!     let vault_size = 16;
[364](https://docs.rs#364)//!
[365](https://docs.rs#365)//!     invoke_signed(
[366](https://docs.rs#366)//!         &create_account(
[367](https://docs.rs#367)//!             &payer.key,
[368](https://docs.rs#368)//!             &vault_pda.key,
[369](https://docs.rs#369)//!             lamports,
[370](https://docs.rs#370)//!             vault_size,
[371](https://docs.rs#371)//!             &program_id,
[372](https://docs.rs#372)//!         ),
[373](https://docs.rs#373)//!         &[
[374](https://docs.rs#374)//!             payer.clone(),
[375](https://docs.rs#375)//!             vault_pda.clone(),
[376](https://docs.rs#376)//!         ],
[377](https://docs.rs#377)//!         &[
[378](https://docs.rs#378)//!             &[
[379](https://docs.rs#379)//!                 b"vault",
[380](https://docs.rs#380)//!                 payer.key.as_ref(),
[381](https://docs.rs#381)//!                 &[vault_bump_seed],
[382](https://docs.rs#382)//!             ],
[383](https://docs.rs#383)//!         ]
[384](https://docs.rs#384)//!     )?;
[385](https://docs.rs#385)//!     Ok(())
[386](https://docs.rs#386)//! }
[387](https://docs.rs#387)//! ```
[388](https://docs.rs#388)//!
[389](https://docs.rs#389)//! # Native programs
[390](https://docs.rs#390)//!
[391](https://docs.rs#391)//! Some solana programs are [_native programs_][np2], running native machine
[392](https://docs.rs#392)//! code that is distributed with the runtime, with well-known program IDs.
[393](https://docs.rs#393)//!
[394](https://docs.rs#394)//! [np2]: https://docs.solanalabs.com/runtime/programs
[395](https://docs.rs#395)//!
[396](https://docs.rs#396)//! Some native programs can be [invoked][cpi] by other programs, but some can
[397](https://docs.rs#397)//! only be executed as "top-level" instructions included by off-chain clients
[398](https://docs.rs#398)//! in a [`Transaction`].
[399](https://docs.rs#399)//!
[400](https://docs.rs#400)//! [`Transaction`]: https://docs.rs/solana-sdk/latest/solana_sdk/transaction/struct.Transaction.html
[401](https://docs.rs#401)//!
[402](https://docs.rs#402)//! This crate defines the program IDs for most native programs. Even though
[403](https://docs.rs#403)//! some native programs cannot be invoked by other programs, a Solana program
[404](https://docs.rs#404)//! may need access to their program IDs. For example, a program may need to
[405](https://docs.rs#405)//! verify that an ed25519 signature verification instruction was included in
[406](https://docs.rs#406)//! the same transaction as its own instruction. For many native programs, this
[407](https://docs.rs#407)//! crate also defines enums that represent the instructions they process, and
[408](https://docs.rs#408)//! constructors for building the instructions.
[409](https://docs.rs#409)//!
[410](https://docs.rs#410)//! Locations of program IDs and instruction constructors are noted in the list
[411](https://docs.rs#411)//! below, as well as whether they are invokable by other programs.
[412](https://docs.rs#412)//!
[413](https://docs.rs#413)//! While some native programs have been active since the genesis block, others
[414](https://docs.rs#414)//! are activated dynamically after a specific [slot], and some are not yet
[415](https://docs.rs#415)//! active. This documentation does not distinguish which native programs are
[416](https://docs.rs#416)//! active on any particular network. The `solana feature status` CLI command
[417](https://docs.rs#417)//! can help in determining active features.
[418](https://docs.rs#418)//!
[419](https://docs.rs#419)//! [slot]: https://solana.com/docs/terminology#slot
[420](https://docs.rs#420)//!
[421](https://docs.rs#421)//! Native programs important to Solana program authors include:
[422](https://docs.rs#422)//!
[423](https://docs.rs#423)//! - __System Program__: Creates new accounts, allocates account data, assigns
[424](https://docs.rs#424)//!   accounts to owning programs, transfers lamports from System Program owned
[425](https://docs.rs#425)//!   accounts and pays transaction fees.
[426](https://docs.rs#426)//!   - ID: [`solana_system_interface::program::ID`](https://docs.rs/solana-system-interface/latest/solana_system_interface/program/constant.ID.html)
[427](https://docs.rs#427)//!   - Instruction: [`solana_system_interface::instruction`](https://docs.rs/solana-system-interface/latest/solana_system_interface/instruction/index.html)
[428](https://docs.rs#428)//!   - Invokable by programs? yes
[429](https://docs.rs#429)//!

[548](https://docs.rs#548)
[549](https://docs.rs#549)/// Convenience macro for doing integer division where the operation's safety
[550](https://docs.rs#550)/// can be checked at compile-time.
[551](https://docs.rs#551)///
[552](https://docs.rs#552)/// Since `unchecked_div_by_const!()` is supposed to fail at compile-time, abuse
[553](https://docs.rs#553)/// doctests to cover failure modes
[554](https://docs.rs#554)///
[555](https://docs.rs#555)/// # Examples
[556](https://docs.rs#556)///
[557](https://docs.rs#557)/// Literal denominator div-by-zero fails:
[558](https://docs.rs#558)///
[559](https://docs.rs#559)/// ```compile_fail
[560](https://docs.rs#560)/// # use solana_program::unchecked_div_by_const;
[561](https://docs.rs#561)/// # fn main() {
[562](https://docs.rs#562)/// let _ = unchecked_div_by_const!(10, 0);
[563](https://docs.rs#563)/// # }
[564](https://docs.rs#564)/// ```
[565](https://docs.rs#565)///
[566](https://docs.rs#566)/// Const denominator div-by-zero fails:
[567](https://docs.rs#567)///
[568](https://docs.rs#568)/// ```compile_fail
[569](https://docs.rs#569)/// # use solana_program::unchecked_div_by_const;
[570](https://docs.rs#570)/// # fn main() {
[571](https://docs.rs#571)/// const D: u64 = 0;
[572](https://docs.rs#572)/// let _ = unchecked_div_by_const!(10, D);
[573](https://docs.rs#573)/// # }
[574](https://docs.rs#574)/// ```
[575](https://docs.rs#575)///
[576](https://docs.rs#576)/// Non-const denominator fails:
[577](https://docs.rs#577)///
[578](https://docs.rs#578)/// ```compile_fail
[579](https://docs.rs#579)/// # use solana_program::unchecked_div_by_const;
[580](https://docs.rs#580)/// # fn main() {
[581](https://docs.rs#581)/// let d = 0;
[582](https://docs.rs#582)/// let _ = unchecked_div_by_const!(10, d);
[583](https://docs.rs#583)/// # }
[584](https://docs.rs#584)/// ```
[585](https://docs.rs#585)///
[586](https://docs.rs#586)/// Literal denominator div-by-zero fails:
[587](https://docs.rs#587)///
[588](https://docs.rs#588)/// ```compile_fail
[589](https://docs.rs#589)/// # use solana_program::unchecked_div_by_const;
[590](https://docs.rs#590)/// # fn main() {
[591](https://docs.rs#591)/// const N: u64 = 10;
[592](https://docs.rs#592)/// let _ = unchecked_div_by_const!(N, 0);
[593](https://docs.rs#593)/// # }
[594](https://docs.rs#594)/// ```
[595](https://docs.rs#595)///
[596](https://docs.rs#596)/// Const denominator div-by-zero fails:
[597](https://docs.rs#597)///
[598](https://docs.rs#598)/// ```compile_fail
[599](https://docs.rs#599)/// # use solana_program::unchecked_div_by_const;
[600](https://docs.rs#600)/// # fn main() {
[601](https://docs.rs#601)/// const N: u64 = 10;
[602](https://docs.rs#602)/// const D: u64 = 0;
[603](https://docs.rs#603)/// let _ = unchecked_div_by_const!(N, D);
[604](https://docs.rs#604)/// # }
[605](https://docs.rs#605)/// ```
[606](https://docs.rs#606)///
[607](https://docs.rs#607)/// Non-const denominator fails:
[608](https://docs.rs#608)///
[609](https://docs.rs#609)/// ```compile_fail
[610](https://docs.rs#610)/// # use solana_program::unchecked_div_by_const;
[611](https://docs.rs#611)/// # fn main() {
[612](https://docs.rs#612)/// # const N: u64 = 10;
[613](https://docs.rs#613)/// let d = 0;
[614](https://docs.rs#614)/// let _ = unchecked_div_by_const!(N, d);
[615](https://docs.rs#615)/// # }
[616](https://docs.rs#616)/// ```
[617](https://docs.rs#617)///
[618](https://docs.rs#618)/// Literal denominator div-by-zero fails:
[619](https://docs.rs#619)///
[620](https://docs.rs#620)/// ```compile_fail
[621](https://docs.rs#621)/// # use solana_program::unchecked_div_by_const;
[622](https://docs.rs#622)/// # fn main() {
[623](https://docs.rs#623)/// let n = 10;
[624](https://docs.rs#624)/// let _ = unchecked_div_by_const!(n, 0);
[625](https://docs.rs#625)/// # }
[626](https://docs.rs#626)/// ```
[627](https://docs.rs#627)///
[628](https://docs.rs#628)/// Const denominator div-by-zero fails:
[629](https://docs.rs#629)///
[630](https://docs.rs#630)/// ```compile_fail
[631](https://docs.rs#631)/// # use solana_program::unchecked_div_by_const;
[632](https://docs.rs#632)/// # fn main() {
[633](https://docs.rs#633)/// let n = 10;
[634](https://docs.rs#634)/// const D: u64 = 0;
[635](https://docs.rs#635)/// let _ = unchecked_div_by_const!(n, D);
[636](https://docs.rs#636)/// # }
[637](https://docs.rs#637)/// ```
[638](https://docs.rs#638)///
[639](https://docs.rs#639)/// Non-const denominator fails:
[640](https://docs.rs#640)///
[641](https://docs.rs#641)/// ```compile_fail
[642](https://docs.rs#642)/// # use solana_program::unchecked_div_by_const;
[643](https://docs.rs#643)/// # fn main() {
[644](https://docs.rs#644)/// let n = 10;
[645](https://docs.rs#645)/// let d = 0;
[646](https://docs.rs#646)/// let _ = unchecked_div_by_const!(n, d);
[647](https://docs.rs#647)/// # }
[648](https://docs.rs#648)/// ```
[649](https://docs.rs#649)#[macro_export]
[650](https://docs.rs#650)macro_rules! unchecked_div_by_const {
[651](https://docs.rs#651)    ($num:expr, $den:expr) => {{
[652](https://docs.rs#652)        // Ensure the denominator is compile-time constant
[653](https://docs.rs#653)        let _ = [(); ($den - $den) as usize];
[654](https://docs.rs#654)        // Compile-time constant integer div-by-zero passes for some reason
[655](https://docs.rs#655)        // when invoked from a compilation unit other than that where this
[656](https://docs.rs#656)        // macro is defined. Do an explicit zero-check for now. Sorry about the
[657](https://docs.rs#657)        // ugly error messages!
[658](https://docs.rs#658)        // https://users.rust-lang.org/t/unexpected-behavior-of-compile-time-integer-div-by-zero-check-in-declarative-macro/56718
[659](https://docs.rs#659)        let _ = [(); ($den as usize) - 1];
[660](https://docs.rs#660)        #[allow(clippy::arithmetic_side_effects)]
[661](https://docs.rs#661)        let quotient = $num / $den;
[662](https://docs.rs#662)        quotient
[663](https://docs.rs#663)    }};
[664](https://docs.rs#664)}
[665](https://docs.rs#665)
[666](https://docs.rs#666)// This re-export is purposefully listed after all other exports: because of an
[667](https://docs.rs#667)// interaction within rustdoc between the reexports inside this module of
[668](https://docs.rs#668)// `solana_program`'s top-level modules, and `solana_sdk`'s glob re-export of
[669](https://docs.rs#669)// `solana_program`'s top-level modules, if this re-export is not lexically last
[670](https://docs.rs#670)// rustdoc fails to generate documentation for the re-exports within
[671](https://docs.rs#671)// `solana_sdk`.
[672](https://docs.rs#672)#[deprecated(since = "2.2.0", note = "Use solana-example-mocks instead")]
[673](https://docs.rs#673)#[cfg(not(target_os = "solana"))]
[674](https://docs.rs#674)pub use solana_example_mocks as example_mocks;
[675](https://docs.rs#675)
[676](https://docs.rs#676)#[cfg(test)]
[677](https://docs.rs#677)mod tests {
[678](https://docs.rs#678)    #[test]
[679](https://docs.rs#679)    fn test_unchecked_div_by_const() {
[680](https://docs.rs#680)        const D: u64 = 2;
[681](https://docs.rs#681)        const N: u64 = 10;
[682](https://docs.rs#682)        let n = 10;
[683](https://docs.rs#683)        assert_eq!(unchecked_div_by_const!(10, 2), 5);
[684](https://docs.rs#684)        assert_eq!(unchecked_div_by_const!(N, 2), 5);
[685](https://docs.rs#685)        assert_eq!(unchecked_div_by_const!(n, 2), 5);
[686](https://docs.rs#686)        assert_eq!(unchecked_div_by_const!(10, D), 5);
[687](https://docs.rs#687)        assert_eq!(unchecked_div_by_const!(N, D), 5);
[688](https://docs.rs#688)        assert_eq!(unchecked_div_by_const!(n, D), 5);
[689](https://docs.rs#689)    }
[690](https://docs.rs#690)}

# solana_program::log - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-program/4.0.0/solana_program/log/index.html

## Expand description

Logging utilities for Rust-based Solana programs.

Logging is the main mechanism for getting debugging information out of running Solana programs, and there are several functions available for doing so efficiently, depending on the type of data being logged.

The most common way to emit logs is through the [ msg!](https://docs.rs/macro.msg.html) macro, which logs
simple strings, as well as

[formatted strings](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/).

Logs can be viewed in multiple ways:

- The `solana logs`command displays logs for all transactions executed on a network. Note though that transactions that fail during pre-flight simulation are not displayed here.
- When submitting transactions via `RpcClient``solana_rpc_client`crate logs at the “debug” level any logs for transactions that failed during simulation. If using`env_logger``RUST_LOG=solana_rpc_client=debug`.
- Logs can be retrieved from a finalized transaction by calling
`RpcClient::get_transaction`
- Block explorers may display logs.

While most logging functions are defined in this module, [ Pubkey](https://docs.rs/solana-address/1.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/solana_address/struct.Address.html)s can
also be efficiently logged with the

[function.](https://docs.rs/solana-address/1.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/solana_address/struct.Address.html#method.log)

`Pubkey::log`## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [msg](https://docs.rs/macro.msg.html)
- Print a message to the log.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [sol_log](https://docs.rs/fn.sol_log.html)
- Print a string to the log.
- [sol_](https://docs.rs/fn.sol_log_64.html)- log_ - 64
- Print 64-bit values represented as hexadecimal to the log.
- [sol_](https://docs.rs/fn.sol_log_compute_units.html)- log_ - compute_ - units
- Print the remaining compute units available to the program.
- [sol_](https://docs.rs/fn.sol_log_data.html)- log_ - data
- Print some slices as base64.
- [sol_](https://docs.rs/fn.sol_log_params.html)- log_ - params
- Print the hexadecimal representation of the program’s input parameters.
- [sol_](https://docs.rs/fn.sol_log_slice.html)- log_ - slice
- Print the hexadecimal representation of a slice.

---

Resize the account’s data: Either truncating or zero extending.

Note:  Account data can be increased within a single call by up to
`solana_program::entrypoint::MAX_PERMITTED_DATA_INCREASE` bytes.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-1)Safety

This method makes assumptions about the layout and location of memory
referenced by `AccountInfo` fields. It should only be called for
instances of `AccountInfo` that were created by the runtime and received
in the `process_instruction` entrypoint of a program.

# Instruction in solana_program::instruction - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-program/4.0.0/solana_program/instruction/struct.Instruction.html

```
pub struct Instruction {
    pub program_id:
```
[Address](https://docs.rs/solana-address/1.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/solana_address/struct.Address.html),
    pub accounts: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[AccountMeta](https://docs.rs/struct.AccountMeta.html)>,
    pub data: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)>,
}## Expand description

A directive for a single invocation of a Solana program.

An instruction specifies which program it is calling, which accounts it may
read or modify, and additional data that serves as input to the program. One
or more instructions are included in transactions submitted by Solana
clients. Instructions are also used to describe [cross-program
invocations](https://solana.com/docs/core/cpi).

During execution, a program will receive a list of account data as one of
its arguments, in the same order as specified during `Instruction`
construction.

While Solana is agnostic to the format of the instruction data, it has
built-in support for serialization via [ borsh](https://docs.rs/borsh/latest/borsh/) and

[.](https://docs.rs/bincode/latest/bincode/)

`bincode`[§](https://docs.rs#specifying-account-metadata)Specifying account metadata

When constructing an [ Instruction](https://docs.rs/struct.Instruction.html), a list of all accounts that may be
read or written during the execution of that instruction must be supplied as

[values.](https://docs.rs/struct.AccountMeta.html)

`AccountMeta`Any account whose data may be mutated by the program during execution must be specified as writable. During execution, writing to an account that was not specified as writable will cause the transaction to fail. Writing to an account that is not owned by the program will cause the transaction to fail.

Any account whose lamport balance may be mutated by the program during
execution must be specified as writable. During execution, mutating the
lamports of an account that was not specified as writable will cause the
transaction to fail. While *subtracting* lamports from an account not owned
by the program will cause the transaction to fail, *adding* lamports to any
account is allowed, as long is it is mutable.

Accounts that are not read or written by the program may still be specified
in an `Instruction`’s account list. These will affect scheduling of program
execution by the runtime, but will otherwise be ignored.

When building a transaction, the Solana runtime coalesces all accounts used
by all instructions in that transaction, along with accounts and permissions
required by the runtime, into a single account list. Some accounts and
account permissions required by the runtime to process a transaction are
*not* required to be included in an `Instruction`s account list. These
include:

- The program ID — it is a separate field of `Instruction`
- The transaction’s fee-paying account — it is added during `Message`

Programs may require signatures from some accounts, in which case they
should be specified as signers during `Instruction` construction. The
program must still validate during execution that the account is a signer.

**crate features **`borsh` and `std` only.

[Source](https://docs.rs/solana-instruction/3.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/solana_instruction/lib.rs.html#151-155)

#### pub fn [new_with_borsh](https://docs.rs#method.new_with_borsh)<T>(
    program_id: [Address](https://docs.rs/solana-address/1.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/solana_address/struct.Address.html),
    data: [&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
    accounts: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[AccountMeta](https://docs.rs/struct.AccountMeta.html)>,
) -> [Instruction](https://docs.rs/struct.Instruction.html)

**crate features**only.

`borsh` and `std`Create a new instruction from a value, encoded with [ borsh](https://docs.rs/borsh/latest/borsh/).

`program_id` is the address of the program that will execute the instruction.
`accounts` contains a description of all accounts that may be accessed by the program.

Borsh serialization is often preferred over bincode as it has a stable
[specification](https://borsh.io/) and an [implementation in JavaScript](https://github.com/near/borsh-js), neither of
which are true of bincode.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
#[derive(BorshSerialize, BorshDeserialize)]
pub struct MyInstruction {
    pub lamports: u64,
}
pub fn create_instruction(
    program_id: &Pubkey,
    from: &Pubkey,
    to: &Pubkey,
    lamports: u64,
) -> Instruction {
    let instr = MyInstruction { lamports };
    Instruction::new_with_borsh(
        *program_id,
        &instr,
        vec![
            AccountMeta::new(*from, true),
            AccountMeta::new(*to, false),
        ],
   )
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/solana-instruction/3.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/solana_instruction/lib.rs.html#202-206)#### pub fn [new_with_bincode](https://docs.rs#method.new_with_bincode)<T>(
